## Abstract

In 2024, Daniel Litt posed a simple coinflip game pitting Alice’s “Heads-Heads” vs Bob’s “Heads-Tails”: who is more likely to win if they score 1 point per occurrence of their substring in a sequence of $n$ fair coinflips? This attracted over 1 million views on X and quickly spawned several articles explaining the counterintuitive solution. We study the generalized game, where the set of coin outcomes, $\{\text{Heads},\text{Tails}\}$ , is generalized to an arbitrary finite alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ , and where Alice’s and Bob’s substrings are any finite $\mathcal{A}$ -strings of the same length. We find that the winner of Litt’s game can be determined by a single quantity which measures the amount of prefix/suffix self-overlaps in each string; whoever’s string has more overlaps loses. For example, “Heads-Tails” beats “Heads-Heads” in the original problem because “Heads-Heads” has a prefix/suffix overlap of length 1 while “Heads-Tails” has none. The method of proof is to develop a precise Edgeworth expansion for discrete Markov chains, and apply this to calculate Alice’s and Bob’s probability to win the game correct to order $O(1/n)$ .

## 1. Introduction

On March 16, 2024 Daniel Litt posted the following brainteaser on X [17]:

Flip a fair coin 100 times—it gives a sequence of heads (H) and tails (T). For each HH in the sequence of flips, Alice gets a point; for each HT, Bob does, so e.g. for the sequence THHHT Alice gets 2 points and Bob gets 1 point. Who is most likely to win?

The post gained popularity due to the deceptively unintuitive nature of the problem, with plurality of respondents in an attached poll believing (incorrectly) that the game is fair, and the correct answer being chosen the least often.

This problem turned out to have a surprisingly rich mathematical structure. In short order, a succession of papers appeared: Ekhad and Zeilberger [5], Segert [26], and Grimmett [8], each of which rigorously analyzed the problem via different techniques (respectively, symbolic computation, asymptotic analysis, and probability theory). We highlight here two key results. Firstly, Litt’s qualitative question “Who is more likely to win” was answered for an arbitrary number $n$ of coin flips: Bob is strictly favored as long as $n$ is at least 3 [26; 8]. Secondly, and more immediately relevant to the present work, for the quantitative question of finding the winning probabilities, the following asymptotic as ${n\to\infty}$ was found by [5; 26; 8] (by different methods):

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Bob wins})-\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Alice wins}) \displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi n}} $$

and, more precisely,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}-\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Alice wins})\sim\frac{3}{4\sqrt{\pi n}},\qquad\frac{1}{2}-\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Bob wins})\sim\frac{1}{4\sqrt{\pi n}}. $$

A natural generalization of Litt’s problem, consider for example by [5], is to let Alice’s and Bob’s strings be arbitrary finite sequences of the same length $\ell$ in an arbitrary finite alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ ; we then assume that Alice and Bob do a generalized coin tossing where a sequence of random letters are generated, with the letters independent and uniformly distributed. (See Section 4 for details. We leave extensions to non-uniform letter distributions to the reader.) We call also this generalization Litt’s game.

This generalization to arbitrary strings was considered by Basdevant et al. [1] who established, by a combinatorial argument, a condition under which such a game is exactly fair (see Remark 1.2 below). The main purpose of the present paper is to establish asymptotics extending (1.1)–(1.2) for the generalized problem.

Somewhat surprisingly, with the exception of a small set of pathological strings, we find that who has the advantage in the generalized Litt’s game depends only on how Alice’s/Bob’s string overlap themselves in their prefixs/suffixes. More precisely, for a string $A=a_{1}a_{2}\ldots a_{\ell}$ of length $\ell$ from an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ with $q$ letters, one can calculate a single quantity $\theta_{AA}\in\mathbb{R}$ that measures the size of the prefix/suffix overlap of $A$ defined as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\Theta(A,A) \displaystyle:=\{1\leqslant k\leqslant\ell-1:a_{\ell-k+1}\dotsm a_{\ell}=a_{1}\dotsm a_{k}\}, \displaystyle\theta_{AA} \displaystyle:=\sum_{k\in\Theta(A,A)}q^{k-\ell}=q^{-\ell}\sum_{k\in\Theta(A,A)}q^{k}. $$

(This is a special case of $\theta_{UV}$ between two strings $U,V$ defined in (4.10).) We will prove the following result, which shows that the asymptotic winner of Litt’s game is determined by comparing the value $\theta_{AA}$ of Alice’s string to $\theta_{BB}$ of Bob’s string; whoever’s $\theta$ overlap value is larger loses Litt’s game asymptotically.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let Alice and Bob play Litt’s game with distinct words $A$ and $B$ of the same length $\ell$ in an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ with $q$ letters, and assume that $n$ letters are chosen at random, uniformly and independently.

Exclude the two cases, both with $q=2$ :

- (i) $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}\mathsf{H}$ for some $\ell\geqslant 2$ (see Example 6.2),

- (ii) $A=\mathsf{H}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}$ (see Example 6.3),

and their variants obtained by interchanging Alice and Bob or $\mathsf{H}$ and $\mathsf{T}$ (or both).

Then, with $\theta_{UU}$ given by (1.4) (or (4.10)) and $\sigma^{2}=\sigma^{2}(A,B)$ given by (4.19), we have $\sigma^{2}>0$ , and

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Alice wins}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AA}-1}{2\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}), \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Bob wins}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\theta_{AA}-\theta_{BB}-1}{2\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}), \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Tie}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}), $$

and thus

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Alice wins})-\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Bob wins}) \displaystyle=\frac{\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AA}}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}). $$

In the two excluded cases, the conclusions (1.5)–(1.7) fail (in somewhat different ways), see Examples 6.2 and 6.3.

#### Remark 1.2.

In particular, Theorem 1.1 shows that the game is fair up to order $n^{-1}$ if and only if $\theta_{AA}=\theta_{BB}$ . This is (in different notation) the condition by Basdevant et al. [1], who showed (by completely different methods) that in this case the game is perfectly fair for every $n$ : $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Alice wins})=\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Bob wins})$ . (The result in [1] is stated for $q=2$ , but the proof holds for an arbitrary finite alphabet.) Our result thus shows that if the condition in [1] is not satisfied, then the game is for all large $n$ not fair; thus their condition for fairness is both necessary and sufficient. $\triangle$

Our method to prove Theorem 1.1 is to recognize (1.5) and (1.6) as examples of (first order) Edgeworth expansions. Edgeworth expansions are useful approximations in many situations in probability and statistics, and they have been rigorously established in many situations, see Section 2.3 for a background. We use a general result giving an Edgeworth expansion for partial sums of an integer-valued function of a finite-state Markov chain. There is a large literature on Edgeworth expansions in various situations, including Markov chains, see Section 2.3. However, we have failed to find a general theorem that is directly applicable here. We therefore state such a theorem for finite-state Markov chains here (in two versions, Theorems 3.2 and 3.4); it is perhaps not new, but since we do not know a reference we give for completeness a complete proof.

## 2. Preliminaries

### 2.1. Notation

The characteristic function of a random variable $X$ is defined by

$$ \displaystyle\varphi(t)=\varphi_{X}(t):=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}e^{\mathrm{i}tX},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}. $$

Vectors are generally regarded as column vectors in formulas using matrix notation; the row vector that is the transpose of a column vector $v$ is denoted $v^{\mathsf{t}}$ .

We let $\boldsymbol{1}=(1,\dots,1)^{\mathsf{t}}$ , the (column) vector with all entries 1, with the dimension of the vector determined by context.

For vectors $v$ (in $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ for some $m\in\mathbb{N}$ ) we let $\lVert v\rVert$ be the usual Euclidean norm. For a square matrix $A$ , let $\lVert A\rVert$ denote its operator norm

$$ \displaystyle\lVert A\rVert:=\sup\bigl\{\lVert Av\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\bigr\} $$

and let $\rho(A)$ denote its spectral norm

$$ \displaystyle\rho(A):=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of $A$}\}. $$

Recall the spectral radius formula

$$ \displaystyle\rho(A)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\lVert A^{n}\rVert^{1/n}. $$

A square matrix $A$ with non-negative entries is irreducible if for every pair of indices $i,j$ we have $(A^{n})_{ij}>0$ for some $n\geqslant 1$ ; the matrix is primitive if we further can choose the same $n$ for all pairs $i,j$ ; see e.g. [27, Chapter 1]. Recall that a matrix is primitive if and only if it is irreducible and aperiodic [27, Theorem 1.4]. A stochastic matrix is a square matrix with non-negative entries where all row sums are 1. It follows from the Perron–Frobenius theorem [27, Theorem 1.5] that an irreducible stochastic matrix has an eigenvalue 1 which is (algebraically) simple, and that the spectral radius is 1; corresponding right and left eigenvectors are $\boldsymbol{1}$ and $\pi^{\mathsf{t}}$ , the stationary distribution of the corresponding Markov chain.

For $z_{0}\in\mathbb{C}$ and $r>0$ , let $D(z_{0},r):=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-z_{0}|<r\}$ , the open disc with centre $z_{0}$ and radius $r$ .

We let $\boldsymbol{1}_{\mathcal{E}}$ denote the indicator of an event $\mathcal{E}$ ; this is thus 1 if $\mathcal{E}$ occurs and 0 otherwise.

$C$ denotes unspecified constants that may vary from one occurrence to the next. They may depend on parameters, and we may write e.g. $C(\delta)$ to stress this.

### 2.2. Cumulants

If $X$ is a random variable, with (for simplicity) all moments finite, then its cumulants (also called semi-invariants) are defined by, for integers $m\geqslant 1$ , recalling (2.1),

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{m}=\kappa_{m}(X):=\mathrm{i}^{-m}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{m}}{\mathrm{d}t^{m}}\log\varphi_{X}(t)\bigr|_{t=0}; $$

in other words, $\log\varphi_{X}(t)$ has the Taylor expansion, for $M\geqslant 1$ and small $t$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\log\varphi_{X}(t)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\kappa_{m}\frac{(\mathrm{i}t)^{m}}{m!}+O(|t|^{M+1}). $$

See for example [9, Section 4.6]. The cumulant $\kappa_{m}$ can be expressed as a polynomial in moments of order at most $m$ . In particular [9, Theorem 4.6.4],

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{1} \displaystyle=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X, \displaystyle\kappa_{2} \displaystyle=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X^{2}]-(\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X)^{2}=\operatorname{Var}(X), \displaystyle\kappa_{3} \displaystyle=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[(X-\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X)^{3}]. $$

Thus $\kappa_{2}$ and $\kappa_{3}$ are simply the corresponding central moments. (Higher cumulants have more complicated formulas.)

### 2.3. Background on Edgeworth expansions

The idea of an Edgeworth expansion (or Edgeworth approximation) [4] is that many random variables in probability theory and statistics have distributions that are approximatively normal, and that the approximation often can be improved by adding extra terms to the normal distribution. It turns out that the natural terms to add are derivatives of the normal density function, with coefficients that are given by some (explicit but a little complicated) polynomials of cumulants $\kappa_{m}$ , $m\geqslant 3$ , divided by powers of the variance. (Part of the motivation is that for a normal random variable, all cumulants $\kappa_{m}=0$ for $m\geqslant 3$ ; thus the cumulants measure in some way deviations from normality. For detailed motivations, see [4] and [2, Chapter 17.6-7].) For a continuous random variable $Z$ , for simplicity normalized to have $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}Z=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}Z=1$ , the one-term Edgeworth appoximation is

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(Z\leqslant x)\approx\Phi(x)+\frac{\kappa_{3}(Z)}{6\sqrt{2\pi}}(1-x^{2})e^{-x^{2}/2},\qquad-\infty<x<\infty, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(x):=\int_{-\infty}^{x}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2}\,\mathrm{d}x $$

is the standard normal distribution function. This approximation can be made rigorous, with error bounds, in many situations. The most important, and archetypical, case is when the random variable $Z$ is a normalized sum ${\widetilde{S}}_{n}:=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\sum_{1}^{n}X_{i}$ of $n$ independent and identially distributed (i.i.d.) random variables $X_{i}$ with $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X_{i}=0$ , $\operatorname{Var}X_{i}=\sigma^{2}$ , and a finite third moment $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}|X_{i}|^{3}$ . Then $\kappa_{3}({\widetilde{S}}_{n})=n^{-1/2}\kappa_{3}(X_{i})/\sigma^{3}$ , and, as shown by [6, Theorem IV.2, p. 49], if the distribution of $X_{i}$ is non-lattice, then (2.10) holds with an error $o(n^{-1/2})$ , i.e., with $S_{n}:=\sum_{1}^{n}X_{i}$ the unnormalized sum,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}\leqslant x\sigma\sqrt{n})=\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}({\widetilde{S}}_{n}\leqslant x)=\Phi(x)+\frac{\kappa_{3}(X_{1})}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{2\pi n}}(1-x^{2})e^{-x^{2}/2}+o\bigl(n^{-1/2}\bigr), $$

uniformly in $x$ . (Note that the right-hand side is $\Phi(x)+O(n^{-1/2})$ uniformly in $x$ , so (2.12) implies, and can be seen as a precise version of, the Berry–Esseen theorem [9, Theorem 7.6.1].) Furthermore, under somewhat stronger conditions, the expansion (2.12) can be continued to any number of terms, where the $m$ th term is of the order $n^{-m/2}$ ; see [6, Theorem IV.1, p. 48] or [23, Theorem VI.4 and (VI.1.13)] for a precise statement and the general form of the terms.

However, in this paper we are interested in integer-valued variables, and then (2.12) is not appropriate, since the right-hand side ignores the jumps in the left-hand side when $x\sigma\sqrt{n}$ is an integer. The correct version of (2.12) for integer-valued $X_{i}$ with $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X_{i}=0$ is

$$ \operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}\leqslant x\sigma\sqrt{n})=\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}({\widetilde{S}}_{n}\leqslant x)=\Phi(x)+\frac{\kappa_{3}(X_{1})}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{2\pi n}}(1-x^{2})e^{-x^{2}/2}\\
+\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n}}\vartheta(x\sigma\sqrt{n})e^{-x^{2}/2}+o\bigl(n^{-1/2}\bigr), $$

where we have added a correction term with

$$ \displaystyle\vartheta(x):=\tfrac{1}{2}-(x-\lfloor x\rfloor), $$

see [6, Theorem IV.3, p. 56] (which also includes the case $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X_{i}\neq 0$ , for simplicity ignored here). See also [6, Theorem IV.4, p. 61] and [23, Theorem VI.6] for the corresponding result with further terms (similar, but more complicated), and [16] for an interpretation of this expansion as a Sheppard’s correction of the version for the continuous (or, more generally, non-lattice) case.

Note that $\vartheta(x)=0$ when $x$ is the midpoint between two consecutive integers. In fact, (2.13) can be regarded as an approximation as in (2.12) of the distribution function of $S_{n}$ interpolated linearly between such half-integer points, see [7, Theorem XVI.4.2].

In the present paper we are interested in the distribution function at or close to the mean, i.e., the case $x\approx 0$ above. Note that if, say, $x\sigma\sqrt{n}=O(1)$ , so $x=O(n^{-1/2})$ , then (2.13) simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}\leqslant x\sigma\sqrt{n})=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}x+\frac{\kappa_{3}(X_{1})}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{2\pi n}}+\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n}}\vartheta(x\sigma\sqrt{n})+O\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr). $$

We remark that under suitable conditions there are also corresponding Edgeworth expansions of the density function (in the absolutely continuous case) or point probabilities (in the discrete case), which refine the local limit theorem in a similar way, see for example [6, Theorem IV.5, p. 63] or [23, Theorem VII.13]; we will not use these expansions here.

In the present paper, we cannot use the basic results above, since the random variable we are interested in is not a sum of i.i.d. variables. Nevertheless, the Edgeworth expansions above have been extended to various other situations, and there is a large literature on Edgeworth expansions under various situations with dependency; we mention only a few references that are closely related to our case, although none of them is directly applicable to it, see further the discussion before Theorem 3.2. We consider below an irreducible finite-state Markov chain, and random variables defined by (3.7). For this case, Siraždinov [29] proved (under some conditions) an Edgeworth expansion for point probabilities (and a Berry–Esseen type estimate for the distribution function). Nagaev [21] considered more general Markov chains, allowing an infinite number of states, and proved Edgeworth expansions for both continuous and discrete cases under some conditions. (For the continuous case, see also [3] with some corrections and improvements.) For the integer-valued case that we are interested in, Hipp [12, Theorem (3.1)] proved an Edgeworth expansion for point probabilities under more general conditions. The variables in our application to Litt’s game are $m$ -dependent, so an alternative approach would be to use results on Edgeworth expansions for sums of $m$ -dependent variables. However, we have not found a suitable such theorem for integer-valued variables; for the non-lattice case, see e.g. Heinrich [11], Rhee [24], and [18]; see also Rinott and Rotar [25] for a more general result, and the further references there.

### 2.4. Group Inverse

If $A$ is a square (possibly singular) matrix, then the group inverse $A^{\mathsf{g}}$ is defined to be the matrix satisfying:

$$ \displaystyle AA^{\mathsf{g}} \displaystyle=A^{\mathsf{g}}A, \displaystyle AA^{\mathsf{g}}A \displaystyle=A, \displaystyle A^{\mathsf{g}}AA^{\mathsf{g}} \displaystyle=A^{\mathsf{g}}, $$

The matrix $A^{\mathsf{g}}$ is unique if it exists, however it may not exist in the first place.

If we regard $A$ as a linear operator in some or $\mathbb{R}^{q}$ (or $\mathbb{C}^{q}$ ), with kernel $\ker(A)$ and range $\operatorname{ran}(A)$ , then $A^{\mathsf{g}}$ exists if and only if $\ker(A)\cap\operatorname{ran}(A)=\{0\}$ and thus $\mathbb{R}^{q}$ (resp. $\mathbb{C}^{q}$ ) is the direct sum $\ker(A)\oplus\operatorname{ran}(A)$ ; in this case $A^{\mathsf{g}}|_{\ker(A)}=0$ and $A^{\mathsf{g}}|_{\operatorname{ran}(A)}$ is the inverse of $A:\operatorname{ran}(A)\to\operatorname{ran}(A)$ .

It can be shown that $A^{\mathsf{g}}$ does exist whenever $A=I-P$ where $P$ is a stochastic matrix, see [19]. In this case, there is actually more that we can say. One useful identity that holds if $P$ is irreducible is

$$ (I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}(I-P)=I-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}} $$

where $\pi$ is the stationary distribution, see Theorem 2.2 in [19].

Most of the time when we want to actually compute $(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}$ , we will use the following well-known representation.

#### Proposition 2.1.

If $P$ is an irreducible stochastic matrix, then

$$ \displaystyle(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle(I-P+\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}})^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{t\nearrow 1}\bigl((I-tP)^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}/(1-t)\bigr). $$

#### Proof.

The first equality is proved in [19]. For the second equality, write

$$ \displaystyle(I-P+\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}})^{-1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{t\nearrow 1}(I-t(P-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}))^{-1} $$

Since for any $t<1$ , the spectral radius of $t(P-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}})$ is $<1$ , the inverse on the right side can be expanded as a geometric series. Moreover, it is easily seen that $(P-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}})^{n}=P^{n}-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}$ for $n\geqslant 1$ , which implies the second equality after a simple calculation. ∎

#### Remark 2.2.

Note that the group inverse does not in general coincide with the more well-known Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse $A^{+}$ . In fact, it can be shown that if $P$ is an irreducible stochastic matrix, then $(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}=(I-P)^{+}$ if and only if the stationary distribution of $P$ is uniform [19, Theorem 6.1]. $\triangle$

## 3. An Edgeworth expansion for finite-state Markov chains

### 3.1. Markov chain preliminaries

Let $(W_{k})_{1}^{\infty}$ be a homogeneous Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{W}$ , with transition probabilities given by the matrix $P=(P_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathcal{W}}$ . (All matrices and vectors in this section will be indexed by $\mathcal{W}$ . The reader that so prefers may without loss of generality assume that $\mathcal{W}=[m]$ for some integer $m$ in this section.) For basic facts on Markov chains used below, see e.g. [22, Chapter 1].

We denote the distribution of $W_{k}$ by

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{k}=(\pi_{k;i})_{i\in\mathcal{W}}\quad\text{where}\quad\pi_{k;i}:=\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(W_{k}=i),\quad i\in\mathcal{W}. $$

In particular, $\pi_{1}$ is the initial distribution of the Markov chain. We regard $\pi_{k}$ as a column vector; recall that its transpose (a row vector) is denoted by $\pi_{k}^{\mathsf{t}}$ . It is well-known that

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{k}^{\mathsf{t}}=\pi_{1}^{\mathsf{t}}P^{k-1},\qquad k\geqslant 1. $$

We say that a sequence $i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell}$ of elements of $\mathcal{W}$ is a path if it can appear with positive probability in the Markov chain, i.e., if $P_{i_{k}i_{k+1}}>0$ for $0\leqslant k<\ell$ . We say that $\ell$ is the length of the path; we denote the length of a path $\mathcal{Q}$ by $\ell(\mathcal{Q})$ . A closed path is a path $i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell}$ such that $i_{\ell}=i_{0}$ . We assume throughout this section that the Markov chain is irreducible, i.e., that

$$ \displaystyle\text{for every pair $i,j\in\mathcal{W}$, there exists a path $i=i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell}=j$
from $i$ to $j$}. $$

We assume also that the Markov chain is aperiodic, i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\gcd\bigl\{\ell(\mathcal{Q}):\mathcal{Q}\text{ is a closed path}\bigr\}=1. $$

It is well-known that our assumptions (3.3)–(3.4) that the Markov chain is irreducible and aperiodic imply that there is a unique stationary distribution $\pi$ , i.e., a distribution satisfying

$$ \displaystyle\pi^{\mathsf{t}}=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}P. $$

Moreover, for any initial distribution $\pi_{1}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{n}\to\pi\qquad\text{as }{n\to\infty}. $$

### 3.2. The main result

Let $g:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$ be an integer-valued function, and define the integer-valued random variables $X_{k}:=g(W_{k})$ and

$$ \displaystyle S_{n}:=\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_{k}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}g(W_{k}). $$

Our goal is to prove an Edgeworth expansion for $S_{n}$ .

We will, besides the aperiodicity condition (3.4), also assume a similar aperiodicity condition for the function $g$ . For a path $\mathcal{Q}$ given by $i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell}$ , define the value of $\mathcal{Q}$ as

$$ \displaystyle g(\mathcal{Q}):=\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}g(i_{k})\in\mathbb{Z}. $$

We then assume:

$$ \displaystyle\text{The set $\bigl\{(g(\mathcal{Q}),\ell(\mathcal{Q})):\mathcal{Q}\text{ is a closed path}\bigr\}$
generates $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ as a group}. $$

#### Remark 3.1.

It is easy to see, arguing similarly as in the proof of Proposition 6.8 below, that in (3.9), it is equivalent to consider only closed paths starting at any given state $i_{0}$ . This implies the following probabilistic formulation of the condition: Start the Markov chain in state $i_{0}$ at time 0, and let $T:=\min\{k\geqslant 1:W_{k}=i_{0}\}$ be the time of the first return there. Then (3.9) is equivalent to:

$$ \displaystyle\text{
The random vector $(S_{T},T)$ is not supported on a proper sublattice of
$\mathbb{Z}^{2}$}. $$

This formulation is used e.g. by [12]. $\triangle$

The following results will be proved in Section 5 . As noted in Section 2.3, there is a large literature on Edgeworth expansions, and in particular Nagaev [21] has proven several similar results for more general Markov chains (allowing also infinite state spaces); however, his theorems for the integer-valued (or, equivalently, lattice-valued) case assume instead of (3.9) a strong aperiodicity condition ([21, Condition C], see Example 6.7) which is not satisfied in our application. Hipp [12, Theorem (3.1)] has, by another method, proven a general result on approximation of the point probabilities using weaker assumptions than [21] and in particular under the same aperiodicity condition (3.9) as we. However, his result is not in a form directly applicable to our probabilities; it seems possible to derive our result from his with some extra work but we have not attempted this; we give instead a direct proof, which also leads to the explicit formulas (3.15)–(3.19) for the parameters (cumulants) in the approximation (3.14) (which are not explicit in [12]). Our proof is similar to the proofs in [21], but much simpler since we consider only finite state spaces; our argument is thus structurally closer to the classical proof of the i.i.d. result using characteristic functions than the arguments by [12].

#### Theorem 3.2.

Let $(W_{k})_{1}^{\infty}$ be a stationary, irreducible and aperiodic homogeneous Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{W}$ , and let $S_{n}$ be defined by (3.7) for some function $g:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$ such that (3.9) holds. Let

$$ \displaystyle\mu \displaystyle:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X_{1}=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}g(W_{1}), \displaystyle\sigma^{2} \displaystyle:=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(S_{n}), \displaystyle\varkappa_{3} \displaystyle:=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\kappa_{3}(S_{n}). $$

(The limits exist and are finite under our assumptions.) Then $\sigma^{2}>0$ , $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}S_{n}=n\mu$ , and with $\Phi(x)$ and $\vartheta(x)$ as in (2.11) and (2.14),

$$ \operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}-n\mu\leqslant x\sigma\sqrt{n})=\Phi(x)+\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{2\pi n}}(1-x^{2})e^{-x^{2}/2}\\
+\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n}}\vartheta(x\sigma\sqrt{n}+n\mu)e^{-x^{2}/2}+O\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr), $$

uniformly in $x\in\mathbb{R}$ and $n\geqslant 1$ . Moreover, $\mu$ , $\sigma^{2}$ , and $\varkappa_{3}$ have the following explicit expressions:

$$ \displaystyle\mu \displaystyle=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}G\boldsymbol{1} \displaystyle\sigma^{2} \displaystyle=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}\left(G^{2}+2GQPG\right)\boldsymbol{1}-\mu^{2} \displaystyle\varkappa_{3} \displaystyle=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}\left(G^{3}+3GQPG^{2}+3G^{2}QPG+6GQPGQPG\right)\boldsymbol{1} \displaystyle\qquad-\mu\left(6\pi^{\mathsf{t}}GQ^{2}PG\boldsymbol{1}+3\sigma^{2}+\mu^{2}\right), $$

where $\pi$ is the stationary distribution of $P$ and $G=\operatorname{Diag}(g(1),\dots,g(m))$ and $Q:=(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}$ . Equivalently, with $Q^{\prime}:=Q-I=(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}-I$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2} \displaystyle=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}(G^{2}+2GQ^{\prime}G)\boldsymbol{1}+\mu^{2} \displaystyle\varkappa_{3} \displaystyle=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}(G^{3}+3GQ^{\prime}G^{2}+3G^{2}Q^{\prime}G+6GQ^{\prime}GQ^{\prime}G)\boldsymbol{1} \displaystyle\qquad+\mu\left(3\pi^{\mathsf{t}}G^{2}\boldsymbol{1}-6\pi^{\mathsf{t}}GQ^{\prime 2}G\boldsymbol{1}+2\mu^{2}\right). $$

The conditions (3.9) and $\sigma^{2}>0$ are discussed further in Section 6.2 and 6.3.

In particular, for the case $\mu=0$ and $x=0$ we obtain the following.

#### Corollary 3.3.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.2, if furthermore $\mu=0$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}\leqslant 0)=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{2\pi n}}+\frac{1}{2\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n}}+O\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}<0)=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{2\pi n}}-\frac{1}{2\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n}}+O\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr). $$

Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}<0)-\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}>0)=\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{3\sigma^{3}\sqrt{2\pi n}}+O\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}=0)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n}}+O\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr). $$

The local limit theorem (3.23) is here shown as a consequence of (3.20)–(3.21), and thus of (3.14). It can also easily be proved directly from the estimates in (5.37) and (5.52) below using Fourier inversion; furthermore, further terms can be obtained as in [6, Theorem IV.5], see [29, Theorem 2].

We can generalize the set-up above and consider a function $g:\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$ of two variables; we then define

$$ \displaystyle S_{n}:=\sum_{k=1}^{n}g(W_{k-1},W_{k}), $$

where we for convenience index the Markov chain as $(W_{k})_{0}^{\infty}$ . We then similarly define, if $\mathcal{Q}$ is the path $i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle g(\mathcal{Q}):=\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}g(i_{k-1},i_{k})\in\mathbb{Z}. $$

#### Theorem 3.4.

Let $(W_{k})_{1}^{\infty}$ be a stationary, irreducible and aperiodic homogeneous Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{W}$ , and let $S_{n}$ be defined by (3.24) for some function $g:\mathcal{W}^{2}\to\mathbb{Z}$ such that (3.9) holds. Then the conclusions of Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 hold. The explicit expressions for the moments are modified accordingly, see Section 8 for details.

For further extensions, see Section 9.

## 4. Coin tossing

We consider in this section Litt’s game, in the general version described in the introduction which is defined as follows.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite alphabet, with $q:=|\mathcal{A}|\geqslant 2$ letters. (We are mainly interested in the case $q=2$ , and then we let $\mathcal{A}=\{\mathsf{H},\mathsf{T}\}$ as in Litt’s original formulation with coin tossing.) Let $\Xi_{n}=\xi_{1}\dotsm\xi_{n}$ be a random word with $n$ letters $\xi_{i}\in\mathcal{A}$ , chosen independently and uniformly at random. Hence, for any given word $a_{1}\dotsm a_{n}$ , the probability

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\xi_{1}\dotsm\xi_{n}=a_{1}\dotsm a_{n})=q^{-n}. $$

Fix two distinct words $A=a_{1}\dotsm a_{\ell}$ and $B:=b_{1}\dotsm b_{\ell}$ of the same length $\ell\geqslant 1$ . The letters in $\Xi_{n}$ are drawn one by one; Alice scores a point when the last $\ell$ letters form $A$ , and Bob scores a point when they form $B$ . Denote their total scores by $S_{A,n}$ and $S_{B,n}$ ; we are interested in the difference $\widehat{S}_{n}:=S_{A;n}-S_{B,n}$ .

To put this into our framework, define for $1\leqslant k\leqslant n-k+1$ the subword

$$ \displaystyle W_{k}:=\xi_{k}\dotsm\xi_{k+\ell-1}\in\mathcal{A}^{\ell}, $$

and for any word $U\in\mathcal{A}^{\ell}$ , define the indicator

$$ \displaystyle I_{U}(V):=\boldsymbol{1}_{U=V},\qquad V\in\mathcal{A}^{\ell}. $$

Then the net score of the $(k+\ell-1)$ th draw (i.e., the $k$ th draw that may score) is

$$ \displaystyle X_{k}:=I_{A}(W_{k})-I_{B}(W_{k}), $$

and thus the final net score is

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{S}_{n}:=\sum_{k=1}^{n-\ell+1}X_{k}. $$

We may as well assume that the random letter $\xi_{i}$ is defined for every $i\geqslant 1$ ; then also $W_{k}$ , $X_{k}$ , and $S_{n}$ are defined for all $k\geqslant 1$ and $n\geqslant\ell$ . It is obvious that the sequence of random words $(W_{k})_{1}^{\infty}$ forms a stationary, homogeneous Markov chain with state space $\mathcal{A}^{\ell}$ ; furthermore, it is easy to see that this chain is irreducible and aperiodic. By comparing (4.5) and (3.7) we see that

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{S}_{n}=S_{n-\ell+1} $$

for the function $g:\mathcal{A}^{\ell}\to\mathbb{Z}$ given by $g:=I_{A}-I_{B}$ . Note that for any fixed word $U\in\mathcal{A}^{\ell}$ and any $k\geqslant 1$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[I_{U}(W_{k})]=\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(W_{k}=U)=q^{-\ell}, $$

and thus

$$ \displaystyle\mu:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}g(W_{1})=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[I_{A}(W_{1})]-\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[I_{B}(W_{1})]=q^{-\ell}-q^{-\ell}=0. $$

We are thus in the setting of Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3, provided that (3.9) holds. All that remains is thus to calculate $\sigma^{2}$ and $\varkappa_{3}$ and to verify (3.9).

We provide two methods, one a direct method that is specific to this application, and a second method that involves the explicit formulas (3.15)–(3.17) for the moments.

We introduce some more notation. For a pair of two words $U=u_{1}\dotsm u_{\ell}$ and $V=v_{1}\dotsm v_{\ell}$ of length $\ell$ , let

$$ \displaystyle\Theta(U,V):=\{1\leqslant k\leqslant\ell-1:u_{\ell-k+1}\dotsm u_{\ell}=v_{1}\dotsm v_{k}\}, $$

i.e., the set of integers $k<n$ such that the words consisiting of the last $k$ letters of $U$ and the first $k$ letters of $V$ are the same; in other words, $U$ and $V$ may be concatenated with an overlap of $k$ letters. (Note that this is not symmetric: in general $\Theta(U,V)\neq\Theta(V,U)$ .) Note that we do not include $\ell$ in $\Theta(U,V)$ , even if $U=V$ . We define also the rational number, which may be called overlap index,

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{UV}:=\sum_{k\in\Theta(U,V)}q^{k-\ell}=q^{-\ell}\sum_{k\in\Theta(U,V)}q^{k}. $$

This is equivalent to the quantity $[U|V]$ defined by Basdevant et al. [1], which plays a key role in their analysis. More precisely, $\theta_{UV}=q^{-\ell}[U|V]$ .

For two fixed words $U,V\in\mathcal{A}^{\ell}$ , and $1\leqslant j\leqslant\ell-1$ , we have $I_{U}(W_{i})I_{V}(W_{i+j})=0$ unless $\ell-j\in\Theta(U,V)$ , and it follows that, since $W_{i}$ and $W_{i+j}$ together contain $\ell+j$ random letters,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}\bigl[I_{U}(W_{i})I_{V}(W_{i+j})\bigr]=\boldsymbol{1}_{\ell-j\in\Theta(U,V)}\,q^{-(\ell+j)}. $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}\bigl[I_{U}(W_{i})I_{V}(W_{i+j})\bigr] \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell-1}\boldsymbol{1}_{\ell-j\in\Theta(U,V)}\,q^{-(\ell+j)} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\boldsymbol{1}_{i\in\Theta(U,V)}\,q^{i-2\ell}=q^{-\ell}\theta_{UV}. $$

We return to $S_{n}$ . We have $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}S_{n}=n\mu=0$ by (4.8) and thus $\operatorname{Var}S_{n}=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[S_{n}^{2}]$ . Furthermore, by the definition (3.7) (or (4.5)–(4.6)) and expanding,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[S_{n}^{2}] \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}X_{j}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}^{2}]+2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n-i}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}X_{i+k}]. $$

If $k\geqslant\ell$ , then $W_{i}$ and $W_{i+k}$ consist of different letters from $\Xi$ , and thus they are independent, which implies $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}X_{i+k}]=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}]\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i+k}]=0$ ; hence it suffices to take $k<\ell$ in the inner sum in (4.13). Furthermore, it is clear that for any fixed $k\geqslant 0$ , the expectation $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}X_{i+k}]$ does not depend on $i$ . Hence, (4.13) yields

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[S_{n}^{2}] \displaystyle=n\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}^{2}]+2n\sum_{k=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}X_{1+k}]+O(1), $$

where the $O(1)$ comes from the missing terms with $0\leqslant n-i<k<\ell$ . Consequently, (3.12) yields

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}^{2}]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}X_{1+k}]. $$

Recalling (4.4), we see that

$$ \displaystyle X_{k}^{2}=I_{A}(W_{k})+I_{B}(W_{k}). $$

Hence, (4.7) yields

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}^{2}]=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[I_{A}(W_{k})]+\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[I_{B}(W_{k})]=2q^{-\ell}. $$

Furthermore, (4.4) and (4.12) yield

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}X_{1+k}]=q^{-\ell}\bigl(\theta_{AA}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}+\theta_{BB}\bigr). $$

We conclude from (4.15) and (4.17)–(4.18) that

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}=2q^{-\ell}\bigl(1+\theta_{AA}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}+\theta_{BB}\bigr). $$

For the third cumulant $\varkappa_{3}$ we argue similarly. First, since $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}S_{n}=0$ , we have $\kappa_{3}(S_{n})=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[S_{n}^{3}]$ , and by expanding followed by combining equal terms,

$$ \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[S_{n}^{3}]=\sum_{i,j,k=1}^{n}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}X_{j}X_{k}]=\sum_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}^{3}]+3\sum_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}^{2}X_{j}]\\
+3\sum_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}X_{j}^{2}]+6\sum_{1\leqslant i<j<k\leqslant n}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{i}X_{j}X_{k}]. $$

Furthermore, all terms in the sums on the right-hand side with $j\geqslant i+\ell$ or $k\geqslant j+\ell$ vanish by independence, and the terms are invariant under a simultaneous shift of the indices. Hence (3.13) yields

$$ \displaystyle\varkappa_{3}=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}^{3}]+3\sum_{s=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}^{2}X_{1+s}]+3\sum_{s=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}X^{2}_{1+s}]+6\sum_{s,t=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}X_{1+s}X_{1+s+t}]. $$

We have $X_{1}^{3}=X_{1}$ , and thus $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}^{3}]=0$ . Furthermore, (4.4) and (4.16) together with (4.12) show that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{s=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}^{2}X_{1+s}] \displaystyle=q^{-\ell}\bigl(\theta_{AA}-\theta_{AB}+\theta_{BA}-\theta_{BB}\bigr), \displaystyle\sum_{s=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}X_{1+s}^{2}] \displaystyle=q^{-\ell}\bigl(\theta_{AA}+\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}-\theta_{BB}\bigr). $$

Arguing as in (4.12) yields, for three fixed words $U,V,T\in\mathcal{A}^{\ell}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j,k=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}\bigl[I_{U}(W_{i})I_{V}(W_{i+j})I_{T}(W_{i+j+k})\bigr] \displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt=\sum_{j,k=1}^{\ell-1}\boldsymbol{1}_{\ell-j\in\Theta(U,V)}\boldsymbol{1}_{\ell-k\in\Theta(U,V)}\,q^{-(\ell+j+k)} \displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt=q^{-\ell}\theta_{UV}\theta_{VT}. $$

Hence, (4.4) yields

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{s,t=1}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[X_{1}X_{1+s}X_{1+s+t}] \displaystyle=q^{-\ell}\bigl(\theta_{AA}\theta_{AA}-\theta_{AA}\theta_{AB}-\theta_{AB}\theta_{BA}+\theta_{AB}\theta_{BB} \displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt{}-\theta_{BA}\theta_{AA}+\theta_{BA}\theta_{AB}+\theta_{BB}\theta_{BA}-\theta_{BB}\theta_{BB}\bigr) \displaystyle\hskip-20.00003pt=q^{-\ell}(\theta_{AA}-\theta_{BB})(\theta_{AA}+\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}). $$

Finally we obtain from (4.21) and (4.22)–(4.25), after some cancellations,

$$ \displaystyle\varkappa_{3}=6q^{-\ell}(\theta_{AA}-\theta_{BB})(1+\theta_{AA}+\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA})=3\sigma^{2}(\theta_{AA}-\theta_{BB}). $$

It is also possible to obtain this result from the explicit moment formulas. Denote by $P_{\ell}$ the transition matrix, indexed by all $q^{\ell}$ strings of length $\ell$ . Here, a transition $U\to V$ exists if and only if the last $\ell-1$ characters of $U$ coincide with the first $\ell-1$ characters of $V$ . It is easy to see that $P_{\ell}$ is primitive and the stationary distribution is uniform: $\pi=q^{-\ell}\boldsymbol{1}$ ; see (4.29) below. The only remaining difficulty in applying the formulas (3.15)–(3.17) is to calculate the group inverse $(I-P_{\ell})^{\mathsf{g}}$ . It turns out that the entries of this matrix coincide with the overlap indices $\theta_{UV}$ , up to a normalization.

#### Proposition 4.1.

The entries of the group inverse $Q:=(I-P_{\ell})^{\mathsf{g}}$ are given by

$$ (I-P_{\ell})^{\mathsf{g}}_{U,V}=\boldsymbol{1}_{U=V}+\theta_{UV}-\ell q^{-\ell} $$

#### Proof.

Introduce the notation $tail_{k}(U)$ for the string obtained by deleting the first $k$ characters of $U$ . Analogously for $head_{k}(U)$ . It is straightforward to see that for any $U,V$ we have

$$ \displaystyle(P^{j})_{U,V} \displaystyle=q^{-j}\boldsymbol{1}_{tail_{j}(U)=head_{j}(V)}, \displaystyle 0\leqslant j<\ell, \displaystyle(P^{j})_{U,V} \displaystyle=q^{-\ell}, \displaystyle j\geqslant\ell. $$

Further,

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{UV} \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{l-1}q^{k-l}\boldsymbol{1}_{tail_{l-k}(U)=head_{l-k}(V)} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{l-1}q^{-j}\boldsymbol{1}_{tail_{j}(U)=head_{j}(V)}=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\ell-1}P^{j}\right)_{U,V}. $$

At this point, the result follows by a simple calculation from the formula $(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}=\lim_{t\nearrow 1}\bigl(\sum_{k\geqslant 0}t^{k}P^{k}-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}/(1-t)\bigr)$ in Proposition 2.1. ∎

In our case, the diagonal matrix $G$ is given by $G_{AA}=1$ , $G_{BB}=-1$ , and $G$ is otherwise zero.

Clearly $\mu=0$ , by (3.11) or (3.15). For $\sigma^{2}$ and $\varkappa_{3}$ we use (3.18)–(3.19), noting that by Proposition 4.1, $Q^{\prime}_{U,V}=\theta_{UV}-\ell q^{-\ell}$ . Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\pi^{\mathsf{t}}GQ^{\prime}G\boldsymbol{1}=q^{-\ell}\boldsymbol{1}^{\mathsf{t}}GQ^{\prime}G\boldsymbol{1}=\theta_{AA}+\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}. $$

Furthermore, evidently $\pi^{\mathsf{t}}G^{2}\boldsymbol{1}=2q^{-\ell}$ . Hence, (3.18) yields

$$ \displaystyle q^{\ell}\sigma^{2} \displaystyle=\boldsymbol{1}^{\mathsf{t}}G^{2}\boldsymbol{1}+2\boldsymbol{1}^{\mathsf{t}}GQ^{\prime}G\boldsymbol{1}+0 \displaystyle=2+2(\theta_{AA}+\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}) $$

in agreement with (4.19). The calculation of the third cumulant (4.26) by this method is similar, and the details are omitted.

We now obtain a preliminary result for Litt’s game. This will be improved to Theorem 1.1 in Section 7 where we identify the cases where the condition (3.9) does not hold.

#### Theorem 4.2.

Let Alice and Bob play Litt’s game above with distinct words $A$ and $B$ of the same length $\ell$ in an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ with $q$ letters, and assume that $n$ letters are chosen at random, uniformly and independently. Assume also that (3.9) holds. Then, with $\theta_{UV}$ and $\sigma^{2}$ given by (4.10) and (4.19), $\sigma^{2}>0$ and

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Alice wins}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AA}-1}{2\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}), \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Bob wins}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\theta_{AA}-\theta_{BB}-1}{2\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}), \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Tie}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}), $$

and thus

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Alice wins})-\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Bob wins}) \displaystyle=\frac{\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AA}}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}). $$

#### Proof.

A consequence of Corollary 3.3, recalling (4.5) and using (4.19) and (4.26) above. ∎

#### Example 4.3 ( $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}$ vs $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}$ ).

Litt’s original game is the case $\mathcal{A}=\{\mathsf{H},\mathsf{T}\}$ , $q=2$ , $\ell=2$ , $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}$ , $B=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}$ of Theorem 1.1. We have $\Theta(A,A)=\Theta(A,B)=\{1\}$ and $\Theta(B,A)=\Theta(B,B)=\emptyset$ , and thus

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{AA}=\theta_{AB}=\tfrac{1}{2},\quad\theta_{BA}=\theta_{BB}=0. $$

Hence, (4.19) yields $\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ , and (1.5)–(1.8) yield (1.1)–(1.2), with error terms $O(n^{-1})$ . $\triangle$

#### Remark 4.4.

We have here represented the score $\widehat{S}_{n}$ using a (finite-state) Markov chain. We may also note that the sequence $X_{k}$ is $(\ell-1)$ -dependent, which means that general results for sums of $m$ -dependent variables can be applied to $\widehat{S}_{n}$ . See e.g. [11; 24; 18] for some related results; however, we have not been able to find a general result that applies to our situation. $\triangle$

## 5. Proof of Theorems 3.2–3.4

### 5.1. A lemma

We will use the following simple uniform version of the spectral radius formula (2.4). We do not know a reference so we give a proof for completeness.

#### Lemma 5.1.

Let $z\mapsto A(z)$ be a continuous square-matrix-valued function defined on some compact set $K$ . Suppose that for some $r>0$ , we have $\rho(A(z))<r$ for every $z\in K$ . Then there exists $\tilde{r}<r$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\lVert A(z)^{n}\rVert\leqslant C\tilde{r}^{n} $$

for some constant $C$ , uniformly for all $z\in K$ and $n\geqslant 1$ .

#### Proof.

Let $z\in K$ , and choose $r_{z}$ with $\rho(A(z))<r_{z}<r$ . Then the assumption and (2.4) show that there exists $N$ such that $\lVert A(z)^{N}\rVert<r_{z}^{N}$ . Since $z\mapsto A(z)$ is continuous, and the operator norm is a continuous functional, it follows that there exists an open neighbourhood $U_{z}$ of $z$ such that for all $w\in U_{z}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lVert A(w)^{N}\rVert<r_{z}^{N}. $$

Since $\lVert AB\rVert\leqslant\lVert A\rVert\cdot\lVert B\rVert$ for two matrices $A$ and $B$ , it follows that for any $w\in U_{z}$ and all $n\geqslant 1$ , by writing $n=kN+\ell$ with $0\leqslant\ell<N$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lVert A(w)^{n}\rVert\leqslant\lVert A(w)^{N}\rVert^{k}\lVert A(w)^{\ell}\rVert\leqslant r_{z}^{kN}\lVert A(w)^{\ell}\rVert\leqslant r_{z}^{n}\max_{0\leqslant\ell<N}\bigl(r_{z}^{-\ell}\lVert A(w)^{\ell}\rVert\bigr). $$

For fixed $\ell$ , $\lVert A(w)^{\ell}\rVert$ is a continuous function of $z$ , and is thus bounded in $K$ . Consequently (5.3) implies that

$$ \displaystyle\lVert A(w)^{n}\rVert\leqslant C_{z}r_{z}^{n} $$

holds for some $C_{z}$ , uniformly for $w\in U_{z}$ and $n\geqslant 1$ . We may cover the compact set $K$ by a finite number of such open sets $U_{z_{i}}$ , $i=1,\dots,M$ ; thus (5.1) follows for all $z\in K$ with $C:=\max_{i}C_{z_{i}}$ and $\tilde{r}:=\max_{i}r_{z_{i}}<r$ . ∎

### 5.2. Proof of Theorem 3.2

We assume in this subsection the assumptions of Theorem 3.2.

For complex $z\neq 0$ , define the matrix

$$ \displaystyle P(z)=(P(z)_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathcal{W}}\quad\text{where}\quad P(z)_{ij}:=P_{ij}z^{g(j)} $$

and the vector

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{1}(z)=(\pi_{1}(z)_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{W}}\quad\text{where}\quad\pi_{1}(z)_{i}:=\pi_{1;i}z^{g(i)}. $$

Note that $P(1)=P$ and $\pi_{1}(1)=\pi_{1}$ . Furthermore, the matrix-valued function $P(z)$ and the vector-valued function $\pi_{1}(z)$ are analytic functions of $z\neq 0$ .

Let

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(z):=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}z^{S_{n}}, $$

i.e., the probability generating function of $S_{n}$ (in a generalized sense since $S_{n}$ may take both positive and negative integer values). Then $G_{n}(z)$ is a well-defined analytic (in fact, rational) function for complex $z\neq 0$ , since $S_{n}$ takes only a finite number of values for each $n$ . Note that for real $t$ ,

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(e^{\mathrm{i}t})=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}e^{\mathrm{i}tS_{n}}=\varphi_{S_{n}}(t), $$

the characteristic function of $S_{n}$ .

We will use the following well-known representation. Recall that $\boldsymbol{1}=(1,\dots,1)$ , the (column) vector with all entries 1.

#### Lemma 5.2.

For any $z\neq 0$ and $n\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(z)=\pi_{1}(z)^{\mathsf{t}}P(z)^{n-1}\boldsymbol{1}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(W_{1}=i_{1},\dots,W_{n}=i_{n})=\pi_{1;i_{1}}P_{i_{1}i_{2}}P_{i_{2}i_{3}}\dotsm P_{i_{n-1}i_{n}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(z)=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}\prod_{k=1}^{n}z^{g(W_{k})}=\sum_{i_{1},\dots,i_{n}\in\mathcal{W}}\pi_{1;i_{1}}z^{g(i_{1})}P_{i_{1}i_{2}}z^{g(i_{2})}\dotsm P_{i_{n-1}i_{n}}z^{g(i_{n})}, $$

which equals the right-hand side of (5.9). ∎

We aim at finding good estimates of the characteristic function $\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)=G_{n}(e^{\mathrm{i}t})$ . We consider first small $t$ . The following asymptotic formula is central in our arguments.

#### Lemma 5.3.

If $\delta\in(0,1)$ is small enough, then there exist analytic functions $\eta(z)$ and $\lambda(z)$ in $D_{\delta}:=D(1,\delta)$ and a constant $c\in(0,1)$ such that for all $z\in D_{\delta}$ and $n\geqslant 1$

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(z)=\eta(z)\lambda(z)^{n}\bigl(1+O(c^{n})\bigr) $$

and, somewhat more precisely,

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(z)=\eta(z)\lambda(z)^{n}\bigl(1+O(c^{n}|z-1|)\bigr). $$

Furthermore, $\lambda(z)$ is an eigenvalue of $P(z)$ , and $\eta(1)=\lambda(1)=1$ .

#### Proof.

Denote the set of eigenvalues of $P(z)$ by $\Lambda(z)$ .

Consider first $z=1$ . The matrix $P(1)=P$ is stochastic, which means that $P\boldsymbol{1}=\boldsymbol{1}$ , i.e., $\boldsymbol{1}$ is a right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. Moreover, by the Perron–Frobenius theorem and our assumptions (3.3)–(3.4), this eigenvalue is simple and all other eigenvalues $\lambda_{i}$ of $P$ satisfy $|\lambda_{i}|<1$ . Let

$$ \displaystyle\rho^{\prime}:=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\Lambda(1)\setminus 1\}<1. $$

Let also $\rho_{0}=(2\rho^{\prime}+1)/3$ and $\rho_{1}:=(1-\rho^{\prime})/3$ . Thus $0<\rho_{0}<1-\rho_{1}<1$ . Furthermore, $P(1)$ has exactly one eigenvalue (viz. 1) in the open disc $D(1,\rho_{1})$ , and all other eigenvalues in the (disjoint) open disc $D(0,\rho_{0})$ . The eigenvalues $\Lambda(z)$ are the roots of the characteristic polynomial of $P(z)$ , and the coefficients in this polynomial are continuous (in fact, analytic) functions of $z$ . Hence it follows that there exists a small $\delta\in(0,1)$ such that if $z\in D_{\delta}$ (i.e., $|z-1|<\delta$ ), then $P(z)$ has exactly 1 simple eigenvalue in $D(1,\rho_{1})$ , and all other eigenvalues in $D(0,\rho_{0})$ . For $z\in D_{\delta}$ , denote the eigenvalue in $D(1,\rho_{1})$ by $\lambda(z)$ . Thus, for $z\in D_{\delta}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\lambda(z)-1|<\rho_{1}\quad\text{and}\quad|\lambda(z)|>1-\rho_{1}>\tfrac{2}{3}. $$

Since $\lambda(z)$ is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial of $P(z)$ , it follows from the implicit function theorem that $\lambda(z)$ is an analytic function of $z\in D_{\delta}$ . Moreover, provided $\delta$ is chosen small enough, the corresponding left and right eigenvectors $u(z)^{\mathsf{t}}$ and $v(z)$ can (and will) be normalized by

$$ \displaystyle u(z)^{\mathsf{t}}\boldsymbol{1}=1=u(z)^{\mathsf{t}}v(z), $$

for every $z\in D_{\delta}$ , and then $u(z)^{\mathsf{t}}$ and $v(z)$ are analytic functions of $z\in D_{\delta}$ . Note that, since $P(1)=P$ , it follows from (3.5) and $P\boldsymbol{1}=\boldsymbol{1}$ that $\lambda(1)=1$ with normalized eigenvectors

$$ \displaystyle u(1)^{\mathsf{t}}=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}\quad\text{and}\quad v(1)=\boldsymbol{1}. $$

Let $z\in D_{\delta}$ and let

$$ \displaystyle\Pi(z):=v(z)u(z)^{\mathsf{t}}; $$

in other words, the matrix $\Pi(z)$ defines the operator $v\mapsto(u(z)^{\mathsf{t}}v)v(z)$ , which is a projection onto the eigenspace spanned by $v(z)$ ; in particular,

$$ \displaystyle\Pi(z)^{2}=\Pi(z). $$

Moreover, $\Pi(z)$ commutes with $P(z)$ and

$$ \displaystyle P(z)\Pi(z)=\Pi(z)P(z)=\lambda(z)\Pi(z). $$

Consequently, by elementary spectral theory,

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{P}(z):=P(z)-\lambda(z)\Pi(z)=(I-\Pi(z))P(z) $$

has the set of eigenvalues $\Lambda(z)\setminus\{\lambda(z)\}\cup\{0\}$ . This set is contained in $D(0,\rho_{0})$ and thus by the definition (2.3) the spectral radius

$$ \displaystyle\rho(\widetilde{P}(z))<\rho_{0}. $$

Consequently, the spectral radius formula (2.4) implies that for some constant $C=C(z)$

$$ \displaystyle\lVert\widetilde{P}(z)^{n}\rVert\leqslant C\rho_{0}^{n}.\qquad n\geqslant 1, $$

By decreasing $\delta$ a little, we may assume that (5.22) holds on $\overline{D_{\delta}}$ , and then, by Lemma 5.1, (5.22) holds uniformly for all $z\in D_{\delta}$ with some $C=C(\delta)$ .

By (5.19)–(5.20), $\widetilde{P}(z)$ and $\Pi(z)$ commute, and $\widetilde{P}(z)\Pi(z)=\Pi(z)\widetilde{P}(z)=0$ . Hence, (5.20) and (5.18) imply

$$ \displaystyle P(z)^{n}=\bigl(\lambda(z)\Pi(z)+\widetilde{P}(z)\bigr)^{n}=\lambda(z)^{n}\Pi(z)+\widetilde{P}(z)^{n}. $$

Consequently, Lemma 5.2 yields, recalling (5.14) and (5.15), for $z\in D_{\delta}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(z) \displaystyle=\pi_{1}(z)^{\mathsf{t}}\bigl(\lambda(z)^{n-1}\Pi(z)+\widetilde{P}(z)^{n-1}\bigr)\boldsymbol{1} \displaystyle=\lambda(z)^{n-1}\pi_{1}(z)^{\mathsf{t}}\Pi(z)\boldsymbol{1}+O(\rho_{0}^{n-1}) \displaystyle=\lambda(z)^{n-1}(\pi_{1}(z)^{\mathsf{t}}v(z))(u(z)^{\mathsf{t}}\boldsymbol{1})+O(\rho_{0}^{n}), \displaystyle=\lambda(z)^{n-1}\Bigl(\pi_{1}(z)^{\mathsf{t}}v(z)+O\bigl(c^{n}\bigr)\Bigr) $$

with $c:=\rho_{0}/(1-\rho_{1})<1$ ; note that the $O$ terms are uniform for $z\in D_{\delta}$ since (5.22) is and $\pi_{1}(z)$ is bounded for $z\in D_{\delta}$ . We may, by decreasing $\delta$ if necessary, assume that $|\pi_{1}(z)^{\mathsf{t}}v(z)|>1/2$ for $z\in D_{\delta}$ , and then (5.24) yields (5.11) with

$$ \displaystyle\eta(z):=\lambda(z)^{-1}\pi_{1}(z)^{\mathsf{t}}v(z). $$

We have noted $\lambda(1)=1$ , and thus (5.25) and (5.16) yield $\eta(1)=\pi_{1}^{\mathsf{t}}\boldsymbol{1}=1$ .

Finally, (5.11) can be written

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert\frac{G_{n}(z)}{\eta(z)\lambda(z)^{n}}-1\right\rvert\leqslant Cc^{n},\qquad z\in D_{\delta},\;n\geqslant 1. $$

The function $G_{n}(z)/\bigl(\eta(z)\lambda(z)^{n}\bigr)-1$ on the left-hand side is analytic and vanishes at $z=1$ ; hence we can divide it by $z-1$ and obtain, by the maximum principle,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert\frac{G_{n}(z)/(\eta(z)\lambda(z)^{n})-1}{z-1}\right\rvert\leqslant Cc^{n},\qquad z\in D_{\delta},\;n\geqslant 1, $$

which is (5.12). ∎

We may assume (and actually already have assumed in the proof) that $\delta$ is so small that $\eta(z)\neq 0$ and $\lambda(z)\neq 0$ in $D_{\delta}$ , and thus $\log\eta(z)$ and $\log\lambda(z)$ are defined there. Let $\delta_{0}$ be so small that if $z$ is a complex number with $|z|<\delta_{0}$ , then $e^{\mathrm{i}z}\in D_{\delta}$ . We then can define the analytic functions, for $|z|<\delta_{0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\psi(z):=\log\lambda\bigl(e^{\mathrm{i}z}\bigr)\quad\text{and}\quad\gamma(z):=\log\eta\bigl(e^{\mathrm{i}z}\bigr). $$

We obtain from (5.12) the estimate

$$ \displaystyle\log G_{n}(e^{\mathrm{i}z})=n\psi(z)+\gamma(z)+O\bigl(|z|c^{n}\bigr),\qquad|z|<\delta_{0}. $$

Note that, recalling (5.8), (5.29) resembles the elementary decomposition of the characteristic function of the sum of i.i.d. variables as a power of the characteristic function of an individual variable, but we have here also two “error terms”.

#### Lemma 5.4.

The cumulants of $S_{n}$ are given by

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{m}(S_{n})=\mathrm{i}^{-m}\psi^{(m)}(0)n+O(1)=\varkappa_{m}n+O(1) $$

for every $m\geqslant 1$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\varkappa_{m}:=\mathrm{i}^{-m}\psi^{(m)}(0). $$

(The implicit constant may depend on $m$ , but not on $n$ .) In particular,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\kappa_{m}(S_{n})}{n}\to\varkappa_{m}\quad\text{as ${n\to\infty}$}. $$

#### Proof.

Since the functions in (5.29) are analytic, we may differentiate an arbitrary number of times, and obtain by (2.5) and Cauchy’s estimate, for every $m\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{i}^{m}\kappa_{m}(S_{n})=\frac{\mathrm{d}^{m}}{\mathrm{d}t^{m}}\log G_{n}(e^{\mathrm{i}t})\bigr|_{t=0}=n\psi^{(m)}(0)+\gamma^{(m)}(0)+O\bigl(c^{n}\bigr), $$

which is a more precise form of (5.30)–(5.31). ∎

We have so far allowed any initial distribution $\pi_{1}$ , but we now, for simplicity, assume that the Markov chain $(W_{n})_{1}^{\infty}$ is stationary, i.e., that the initial distribution $\pi_{1}=\pi$ , and thus $\pi_{k}=\pi$ for every $k$ by (3.2) and (3.5). Then the random variables $X_{k}$ have the same distribution. As in (3.11), denote their mean by

$$ \displaystyle\mu:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X_{k}. $$

#### Corollary 5.5.

Suppose that the Markov chain $(W_{n})_{1}^{\infty}$ is stationary. Then

$$ \displaystyle\varkappa_{1}=\mu,\qquad\psi^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{i}\mu,\qquad\gamma^{\prime}(0)=0. $$

#### Proof.

Since the random variables $X_{k}$ have the same distribution, (2.7) yields

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{1}(S_{n})=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}S_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X_{k}=n\mu. $$

The result follows from the case $m=1$ of (5.32) and (5.33). ∎

We are now prepared to prove the estimate of $\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)$ that we need for small $t$ .

#### Lemma 5.6.

Suppose that the Markov chain $(W_{n})_{1}^{\infty}$ is stationary. Then there exists $\delta>0$ such that, if $|t|\leqslant\delta$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{S_{n}}(t) \displaystyle=e^{\mathrm{i}n\mu t-n{\varkappa_{2}}t^{2}/2}\Bigl(1-\mathrm{i}n\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6}t^{3}\Bigr)+O\bigl((t^{2}+n^{2}t^{6})e^{-n\varkappa_{2}t^{2}/4}\bigr). $$

#### Proof.

Let $\delta<\delta_{0}$ . Then (5.8), (5.29) and Cauchy’s estimate yield, for $|t|\leqslant\delta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}^{4}}{\mathrm{d}t^{4}}\log\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}^{4}}{\mathrm{d}t^{4}}\log G_{n}(e^{\mathrm{i}t})=n\psi^{(4)}(t)+\gamma^{(4)}(t)+O\bigl(c^{n}\bigr)=O(n). $$

Consequently, a Taylor expansion as in (2.6) yields, using $\varphi_{S_{n}}(1)=1$ , (5.36) and (5.30), for $|t|\leqslant\delta$ and $n\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\log\varphi_{S_{n}}(t) \displaystyle=\mathrm{i}\kappa_{1}(S_{n})t-\frac{\kappa_{2}(S_{n})}{2}t^{2}-\mathrm{i}\frac{\kappa_{3}(S_{n})}{6}t^{3}+O(nt^{4}) \displaystyle=\mathrm{i}n\mu t-n\frac{\varkappa_{2}}{2}t^{2}-\mathrm{i}n\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6}t^{3}+O(t^{2}+nt^{4}). $$

Hence,

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\mathrm{i}n\mu t+n\varkappa_{2}t^{2}/2}\varphi_{S_{n}}(t) \displaystyle=\exp\Bigl(-\mathrm{i}n\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6}t^{3}+O(t^{2}+nt^{4})\Bigr). $$

If $\delta$ is small enough, then the real part of the argument of the exponential function in (5.40) is less than $n{\varkappa_{2}}t^{2}/4+C$ , and consequently, by a Taylor expansion,

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\mathrm{i}n\mu t+n\varkappa_{2}t^{2}/2}\varphi_{S_{n}}(t) \displaystyle=1-\mathrm{i}n\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6}t^{3}+O(t^{2}+nt^{4})+O\Bigl(\bigl(n|t|^{3}+t^{2}\bigr)^{2}e^{n{\varkappa_{2}}t^{2}/4}\Bigr), $$

which yields (5.37), recalling that $|t|=O(1)$ and noting $nt^{4}\leqslant(t^{2}+n^{2}t^{6})/2$ . ∎

We turn to estimating $\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)$ for larger $t$ , and again begin by studying the matrix $P(z)$ . This is where we use our assumption (3.9).

#### Lemma 5.7.

If $0<|t|\leqslant\pi$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\rho\bigl(P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})\bigr)<1. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})$ , and let $u^{\mathsf{t}}=(u_{j})_{1}^{n}$ be a corresponding left eigenvector. Then

$$ \displaystyle\lambda u_{k}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{W}}u_{j}P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})_{jk}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{W}}u_{j}P_{jk}e^{\mathrm{i}g(k)t},\qquad k\in\mathcal{W}, $$

and thus, by the triangular inequality,

$$ \displaystyle|\lambda|\,|u_{k}|\leqslant\sum_{j\in\mathcal{W}}|u_{j}|P_{jk},\qquad k\in\mathcal{W}. $$

Summing over all $k\in\mathcal{W}$ yields, since $(P_{jk})$ is a stochastic matrix,

$$ \displaystyle|\lambda|\sum_{k\in\mathcal{W}}|u_{k}|\leqslant\sum_{j\in\mathcal{W}}|u_{j}|\sum_{k\in\mathcal{W}}P_{jk}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{W}}|u_{j}|. $$

Consequently, $|\lambda|\leqslant 1$ .

Suppose now, to obtain a contradiction, that $|\lambda|=1$ . We then have equality in (5.45), and thus in (5.44) for every $k$ . Note first that since $(P_{jk})$ is irreducible, it follows easily from equality in (5.44) that we have $|u_{k}|>0$ for every $k\in\mathcal{W}$ . Furthermore, equality when applying the triangle inequality to (5.43) implies

$$ \displaystyle\frac{u_{j}e^{\mathrm{i}g(k)t}}{\lambda u_{k}}>0 $$

for all $j,k\in\mathcal{W}$ such that $P_{jk}>0$ . It follows that for any path $\mathcal{Q}$ given by $i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{u_{i_{0}}e^{\mathrm{i}g(\mathcal{Q})t}}{\lambda^{\ell(\mathcal{Q})}u_{i_{\ell}}}=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell}\frac{u_{i_{k-1}}e^{\mathrm{i}g(i_{k})t}}{\lambda u_{i_{k}}}>0 $$

and in particular, for a closed path $\mathcal{Q}$

$$ \displaystyle e^{\mathrm{i}g(\mathcal{Q})t}\lambda^{-\ell(\mathcal{Q})}=\frac{e^{\mathrm{i}g(\mathcal{Q})t}}{\lambda^{\ell}(\mathcal{Q})}>0. $$

Furthermore, $|e^{\mathrm{i}g(\mathcal{Q})t}|=|\lambda^{\ell}(\mathcal{Q})|=1$ , and thus, for every closed path $\mathcal{Q}$

$$ \displaystyle e^{\mathrm{i}g(\mathcal{Q})t}\lambda^{-\ell(\mathcal{Q})}=1. $$

The set of all $(k,\ell)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle e^{\mathrm{i}kt}\lambda^{-\ell}=1 $$

is a subgroup, and thus it follows from (3.9) and (5.49) that (5.50) holds for all $(k,\ell)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ . Taking $(k,\ell)=(1,0)$ , this shows $e^{\mathrm{i}t}=1$ , which contradicts the assumption on $t$ .

This contradiction shows that $|\lambda|<1$ for every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})$ , which is the same as (5.42) by (2.3). ∎

#### Lemma 5.8.

For every $\delta>0$ , there exist $r=r(\delta)<1$ and $C$ such that if $\delta\leqslant|t|\leqslant\pi$ and $n\geqslant 1$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\lVert P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})^{n}\rVert\leqslant Cr^{n}. $$

#### Proof.

A consequence of Lemmas 5.7 and 5.1, taking $K:=\{t\in\mathbb{R}:\delta\leqslant|t|\leqslant\pi\}$ . ∎

#### Lemma 5.9.

For every $\delta>0$ , there exist $r=r(\delta)<1$ and $C$ such that if $\delta\leqslant|t|\leqslant\pi$ and $n\geqslant 1$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\bigl\lvert\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)\bigr\rvert\leqslant Cr^{n}. $$

#### Proof.

A consequence of Lemmas 5.8 and 5.2 together with (5.8). ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.2.

The limits (3.12) and (3.13) exist by (5.32); note that $\sigma^{2}=\varkappa_{2}$ . We postpone the proof that $\sigma^{2}>0$ to Corollary 6.10 in Section 6. Define the normalized variable ${\widetilde{S}}_{n}:=(S_{n}-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt{n})$ which has mean $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}{\widetilde{S}}_{n}=0$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}({\widetilde{S}}_{n})=1+O(1/n)$ by (5.36) and (5.30).

Using the estimates of $\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)$ in Lemmas 5.6 and 5.9, the result (3.14) follows as the classical corresponding result for sums of i.i.d. random variables [6, Theorem IV.3]. There are actually two proofs of this theorem in [6]. We use the second proof in [6, pp. 64–65], taking there

$$ \displaystyle f_{n}(t):=\varphi_{{\widetilde{S}}_{n}}(t)=e^{-\mathrm{i}\mu\sqrt{n}t/\sigma}\varphi_{S_{n}}\Bigl(\frac{t}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\Bigr). $$

We further take $T_{3\,n}$ there as $\delta\sqrt{n}$ with the same $\delta$ as in Lemma 5.6, and we have $d=1$ and $t_{0}=2\pi$ . A crucial part of the estimate is that Lemma 5.6 yields

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{{\widetilde{S}}_{n}}(t) \displaystyle=e^{-t^{2}/2}\Bigl(1-\mathrm{i}\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{n}}t^{3}\Bigr)+O\bigl(n^{-1}(t^{2}+t^{6})e^{-t^{2}/4}\bigr),\qquad|t|\leqslant\delta\sigma\sqrt{n}, $$

and thus, with $g(t):=e^{-t^{2}/2}\bigl(1-\mathrm{i}\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{n}}t^{3}\bigr)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{-\delta\sigma\sqrt{n}}^{\delta\sigma\sqrt{n}}\left\lvert\frac{\varphi_{{\widetilde{S}}_{n}}(t)-g(t)}{t}\right\rvert\,\mathrm{d}t=O\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr), $$

which implies that $I_{2}^{\prime}=O(n^{-1})$ on [6, p. 65]. The rest of the estimates in [6, pp. 64–65] hold without changes, and we obtain (3.14); we omit the details. We may also use the first proof in [6, pp. 57–59], again using (5.55); however, this yields (3.14) with the slightly weaker error term $O\bigl(\frac{\log n}{n}\bigr)$ from the estimates of $I_{k}^{\prime}$ and $\varepsilon_{1}$ on [6, p. 59].

It remains to verify the matrix-based cumulant formulas (3.15)–(3.19). By Lemma 5.4 and (5.28), the cumulants are given in terms of the first three derivatives of $\psi(z)=\log\lambda(e^{iz})$ at $z=0$ . By analyticity of $\lambda(e^{iz})$ , it is enough to calculate the derivatives of $\log\lambda(e^{t})$ where $t$ is real. This can be done by repeated differentiation of the eigenvalue equation and some algebra, see Appendix A, but we will here instead make use of [10], which studies this problem in great generality; in particular, [10, Theorem 4.1] (with a correction of the sign of $\rho_{3}$ ) provides for $P$ as above and any matrix $E$ and small $t$ , the Taylor series

$$ \displaystyle\lambda(P+tE)=1+t\rho_{1}(E)+t^{2}\rho_{2}(E)+t^{3}\rho_{3}(E)+O(t^{4}), $$

where $\lambda(P+tE)$ denotes the largest eigenvalue, and $\rho_{i}$ are the following expressions:

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{1}(E) \displaystyle=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}E\boldsymbol{1}, \displaystyle\rho_{2}(E) \displaystyle=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}EQE\boldsymbol{1}, \displaystyle\rho_{3}(E) \displaystyle=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}EQEQE\boldsymbol{1}-\rho_{1}(E)\cdot\pi^{\mathsf{t}}EQ^{2}E\boldsymbol{1}. $$

Here, as before, we set $Q:=(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}$ . (Recall that since $P$ is irreducible, it has a simple largest eigenvalue; by continuity, this holds also for all small perturbations.) We will use this result in a different, more general form. The expansion (5.56) holds uniformly for all matrices $E$ in a bounded set. (This follows e.g. since the implicit function theorem implies that the eigenvalue $\lambda(P+tE)$ is (for small $t$ ) an analytic function of the entries in $tE$ .) Consequently, (5.56) holds also for a continuous matrix-valued function $E(t)$ . Let $F(t)$ be a smooth one-parameter family of matrices with $F(0)=P$ and take $E(t):=(F(t)-F(0))/t$ (with $E(0):=F^{\prime}(0)$ ); then (5.56) gives an expansion of $\lambda(F(t))$ . We want to extract the first three derivatives at the origin. For this purpose, it is sufficient to replace $F(t)$ with its third-order Taylor series $P+tF^{\prime}(0)+\frac{1}{2}t^{2}F^{\prime\prime}(0)+\frac{1}{6}t^{3}F^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)$ , which gives

$$ \displaystyle E(t):=F^{\prime}(0)+\frac{1}{2}tF^{\prime\prime}(0)+\frac{1}{6}t^{2}F^{\prime\prime\prime}(0). $$

By substituting (5.60) in (5.56)–(5.59), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\lambda(F(t)) \displaystyle=1+t\rho_{1}(E(t))+t^{2}\rho_{2}(E(t))+t^{3}\rho_{3}(E(t))+O(t^{4}) \displaystyle=1+m_{1}t+\tfrac{1}{2}m_{2}t^{2}+\tfrac{1}{6}m_{3}t^{3}+O(t^{4}), $$

where, collecting terms,

$$ \displaystyle m_{1} \displaystyle:=[t^{1}]\lambda(F(t))=[t^{0}]\rho_{1}(E(t))=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1}, \displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}m_{2} \displaystyle:=[t^{2}]\lambda(F(t))=[t^{1}]\rho_{1}(E(t))+[t^{0}]\rho_{2}(E(t)) \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1}+\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(0)QF^{\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1}, \displaystyle\tfrac{1}{6}m_{3} \displaystyle:=\lambda(F(t))[t^{3}]=[t^{2}]\rho_{1}(E(t))+[t^{1}]\rho_{2}(E(t))+[t^{0}]\rho_{3}(E(t)) \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{6}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1}+\tfrac{1}{2}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(0)QF^{\prime\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1}+\tfrac{1}{2}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime}(0)QF^{\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1} \displaystyle\qquad+\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(0)QF^{\prime}(0)QF^{\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1}-\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1}\cdot\pi^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(0)Q^{2}F^{\prime}(0)\boldsymbol{1}. $$

In our case, we set $F(t)=P(e^{t})$ , and it is easy to see from (5.5) that the derivatives are given by $F^{(k)}(0)=PG^{k}$ where $G=\operatorname{Diag}(g(1),\dots,g(m))$ . Furthermore, the relation between the raw moments $m_{i}={\frac{d^{i}}{dt^{i}}}\big|_{t=0}\lambda(F(t))$ and cumulants $\varkappa_{i}={\frac{d^{i}}{dt^{i}}}\big|_{t=0}\log\lambda(F(t))$ is as usual:

$$ \displaystyle\mu=\varkappa_{1} \displaystyle=m_{1}, \displaystyle\sigma^{2}=\varkappa_{2} \displaystyle=m_{2}-m_{1}^{2}, \displaystyle\varkappa_{3} \displaystyle=m_{3}-3m_{2}m_{1}+2m_{1}^{3}. $$

Plugging in (5.62)–(5.64), and recalling $\pi^{\mathsf{t}}P=\pi^{\mathsf{t}}$ , we get the indicated expressions in equations (3.15)–(3.17).

Finally, (2.19) yields

$$ \displaystyle QP=Q-I+\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}=Q^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}, $$

and as a consequence, since $Q\boldsymbol{1}=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Q^{2}P=Q(QP)=Q(Q^{\prime}+\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}})=QQ^{\prime}=Q^{\prime 2}+Q^{\prime}. $$

Substituting these in (3.16)–(3.17) yields (3.18)–(3.19). ∎

We obtain (3.20) directly from (3.14) by taking $\mu=0$ and $x=0$ , noting that $\vartheta(0)=1/2$ by (2.14). To obtain (3.21) we instead take $x<0$ and let $x\nearrow 0$ , noting that $\vartheta(0-)=-1/2$ .

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}<0)-\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}>0)=\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}_{n}(S_{n}<0)+\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}\leqslant 0)-1, $$

### 5.3. Proof of Theorem 3.4

#### Proof of Theorem 3.4.

Let $\widehat{W}_{k}:=(W_{k-1},W_{k})$ ; this is easily seen to be a Markov chain in the state space

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{W}}:=\bigl\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{W}^{2}:P_{ij}>0\bigr\}. $$

We can regard $g$ as a function $\widehat{\mathcal{W}}\to\mathbb{Z}$ , and then the definition (3.24) yields the same $S_{n}$ as (3.7) for the chain $(\widehat{W}_{k})_{1}^{\infty}$ .
