## 6. The aperiodicity condition and non-degeneracy

The general results above use the aperiodicity condition (3.9). In this section we give several equivalent forms of it, and also of the condition $\sigma^{2}>0$ which, as stated in Theorem 3.2 is a consequence. We consider irreducible and aperiodic finite-state Markov chains as in Section 3. In particular, we specialize to Litt’s game, and show that these conditions are always satisfied except for the rather trivial cases in Examples 6.2, 6.3, and 6.4 below.

### 6.1. Bad examples

We begin with a few examples where (3.9) fails, illustrating the reasons for it and showing the consequences. The first two examples are degenerate with also $\sigma^{2}=0$ .

#### Example 6.1.

Consider Litt’s game with $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}\mathsf{H}$ . It is then obvious by induction that

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{S}_{n}=\boldsymbol{1}_{\xi_{n}=\mathsf{T}}-\boldsymbol{1}_{\xi_{1}=\mathsf{T}}\in\{-1,0,1\}. $$

Thus (3.12) yields $\sigma^{2}=0$ . Furthermore, it is easily seen that $g(\mathcal{Q})=0$ for every closed path $\mathcal{Q}$ , and thus (3.9) fails. It is easy to see that the matrix $P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})$ in Section 5 has an eigenvalue $\lambda(e^{\mathrm{i}t})=1$ for every real $t$ , and thus Lemmas 5.7–5.9 fail. It follows trivially from (6.1) that for every $n\geqslant 2$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Alice wins})=\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm Bob wins})=\tfrac{1}{4},\qquad\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\text{\rm tie})=\tfrac{1}{2}. $$

Hence, (1.5)–(1.7) utterly fail, while (1.8) holds trivially. $\triangle$

#### Example 6.2.

More generally, let $\ell\geqslant 2$ and consider Litt’s game with $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}\mathsf{H}$ . Then Alice scores when a run of at least $\ell-1$ tails has begun, and Bob scores when such a run ends, and again it is obvious that $\widehat{S}_{n}\in\{-1,0,1\}$ . Thus $\sigma^{2}=0$ . Also, again $g(\mathcal{Q})=0$ for every closed path $\mathcal{Q}$ , and (3.9) fails. As in Example 6.1, it is easy to see that (1.5)–(1.7) fail, while (1.8) holds trivially by symmetry (reversing the order of the coin tosses, cf. [8]).

We will see below (Theorem 7.1) that, as stated without proof in [1], this example and its obvious equivalent variants obtained by interchanging Alice and Bob or $\mathsf{H}$ and $\mathsf{T}$ (or both) are the only cases in Litt’s game where $\sigma^{2}=0$ . $\triangle$

In the following examples, (3.9) fails but $\sigma^{2}>0$ . We will see that Lemma 5.7 fails for them, and as a consequence also Lemma 5.8; not surprisingly also Lemma 5.9 fails.

#### Example 6.3.

Consider the trivial case of Litt’s game with $\ell=1$ , $A=\mathsf{H}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}$ . In this case, $S_{n}$ is just the number of heads minus the number of tails. Thus,

$$ \displaystyle S_{n}=2S^{\prime}_{n}-n\quad\text{with}\quad S^{\prime}_{n}\in\operatorname{Bin}(n,\tfrac{1}{2}). $$

In particular $S_{n}\equiv n\pmod{2}$ and thus $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}=0)=0$ when $n$ is odd, so (1.7) fails, and consequently (by symmetry) also (1.5)–(1.6) fail. (Asymptotic expansions of the probabilities are easily obtained from (6.3), treating $n$ even and $n$ odd separately; we leave this to the reader.)

Similarly, $g(\mathcal{Q})\equiv\ell(\mathcal{Q})\pmod{2}$ for every path $\mathcal{Q}$ (closed or not). As a consequence, (3.9) does not hold, which is the reason why Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 do not apply. We have $\sigma^{2}=1>0$ by (4.19) (or as a consequence of (6.3)). In the arguments in Section 5, we have by (5.5)

$$ \displaystyle P(z)=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}z&z^{-1}\\
z&z^{-1}\end{pmatrix}. $$

This matrix has rank 1, with eigenvalues $(z+z^{-1})/2$ and 0, and it follows easily from (5.8) and (5.14) that

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)=G_{n}(e^{\mathrm{i}t})=\pi_{1}(e^{\mathrm{i}t})^{\mathsf{t}}P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})^{n-1}\boldsymbol{1}=\cos^{n}t, $$

which of course also follows directly from (6.3). Note that $P(-1)$ has an eigenvalue $-1$ , which means that Lemmas 5.7 and 5.8 do not hold for $t=\pi$ ; similarly, (6.5) shows that Lemma 5.9 fails for $t=\pi$ . $\triangle$

#### Example 6.4.

Consider Litt’s game with $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}\mathsf{T}$ . This game is obviously fair by symmetry, so (1.8) holds trivially (with $\theta_{AA}=\theta_{BB}=\frac{1}{2}$ ), and it is checked below that (1.5)–(1.7) also hold. Thus the conclusions of Theorem 1.1 hold; nevertheless, Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 do not apply because (3.9) does not hold. In fact, if we instead use the alphabet $\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\}$ , we have, recalling (4.2),

$$ \displaystyle g(W_{k})=\pm\boldsymbol{1}_{\xi_{k}=\xi_{k+1}}\equiv\xi_{k}-\xi_{k+1}+1\pmod{2}, $$

and consequently, $g(\mathcal{Q})\equiv\ell(\mathcal{Q})\pmod{2}$ for every closed path $\mathcal{Q}$ , which shows that (3.9) does not hold.

In this case, it is easy to calculate the distribution of $\widehat{S}_{n+1}=S_{n}$ exactly using the arguments in Section 5. We may simplify the calculations by letting $(W_{k})$ be a sequence of i.i.d. random bits with $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(W_{k}=0)=\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(W_{k}=1)=\frac{1}{2}$ , which is a trivial Markov chain, and use the version (3.24) with $g(i,j):=\boldsymbol{1}_{i=j=0}-\boldsymbol{1}_{i=j=1}$ . It is easily seen that for this version, (5.9) is modified to

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(z)=\pi_{0}^{\mathsf{t}}P(z)^{n}\boldsymbol{1} $$

with

$$ \displaystyle P(z):=\bigl(P_{ij}z^{g(i,j)}\bigr)_{i,j\in\mathcal{W}}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}z&1\phantom{{}^{-1}}\\
1&z^{-1}\end{pmatrix}. $$

This matrix has rank 1, with eigenvalues $(z+z^{-1})/2$ and 0 (just as (6.4)), and it follows that, for $n\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})^{n}=(\cos t)^{n-1}P(e^{\mathrm{i}t}). $$

Hence, (6.7) yields

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)=G_{n}(e^{\mathrm{i}t})=\frac{1+\cos t}{2}\cos^{n-1}t. $$

(This factorization has the probabilistic interpretation that $S_{n}$ has the same distribution as a sum $\sum_{0}^{n-1}Y_{j}$ of independent random variables, where $Y_{0}+1$ has the binomial distribution $\operatorname{Bin}(2,\frac{1}{2})$ and $Y_{j}=\pm 1$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each for $j\geqslant 1$ .) It follows easily that, for example, with $m:=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}=0)=2^{-2m-1}\binom{2m}{m}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi n}}+O(n^{-3/2}). $$

We have $\sigma^{2}=1$ , by (4.19) or directly from (6.10) which implies that $\operatorname{Var}S_{n}=n-\frac{1}{2}$ . Hence (1.7) holds, and thus (by symmetry) also (1.5)–(1.6).

This is as expected, but note that the next term in the expansion (6.11), of order $n^{-3/2}$ , will depend on the parity of $n$ . The reason is that the matrix $P(e^{\mathrm{i}\pi})=P(-1)$ has an eigenvalue $-1$ on the unit circle; thus, although the characteristic function (6.10) vanishes at $t=\pi$ , it is not exponentially small for $t$ close to $\pi$ , as it is in Section 5 when we assume (3.9) and as a consequence Lemma 5.7 holds. $\triangle$

We end with an (artificial) example of a different type of Markov chain where (3.9) fails.

#### Example 6.5.

Consider a stationary Markov chain $(W_{k})$ with 4 states $\mathcal{A}=\{a,b,c,d\}$ and the transition matrix

$$ \displaystyle P=\begin{pmatrix}0.45&0.45&0.1&0\\
0.45&0.45&0.1&0\\
0&0&0&1\\
0.5&0.5&0&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

This is irreducible and aperiodic, with stationary distribution $(\frac{5}{12},\frac{5}{12},\frac{1}{12},\frac{1}{12})$ . Let $g(a)=1$ , $g(b)=-1$ , $g(c)=g(d)=0$ . If we partition $\mathcal{W}$ as $\{a,b,d\}\cup\{c\}$ , then $g(W_{k})=0$ if $W_{k-1}$ and $W_{k}$ are in different parts, but $g(W_{k})=\pm 1$ if $W_{k-1}$ and $W_{k}$ are in the same part, and it follows that

$$ \displaystyle g(W_{k})\equiv\boldsymbol{1}_{W_{k}=c}-\boldsymbol{1}_{W_{k-1}=c}+1\pmod{2}. $$

This implies that for any closed path $\mathcal{Q}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle g(\mathcal{Q})\equiv\ell(\mathcal{Q})\pmod{2}, $$

and thus (3.9) does not hold. It is easy to see, e.g. by the calculations below or by Proposition 6.8, that $\sigma^{2}>0$ .

It follows also from (6.13) and induction that

$$ \displaystyle S_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}g(W_{k})\equiv\boldsymbol{1}_{W_{1}=d}+\boldsymbol{1}_{W_{n}=c}+n\pmod{2}. $$

As ${n\to\infty}$ , $W_{1}$ and $W_{n}$ are asymptotically independent, and thus $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(W_{1}=d,W_{n}=c)\to\frac{1}{12^{2}}$ and $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(W_{1}\neq d,W_{n}\neq c)\to\frac{11^{2}}{12^{2}}$ . Hence, if $n$ is even, then $S_{n}$ is even with probability $\approx\frac{122}{144}=\frac{61}{72}$ , while if $n$ is odd then $S_{n}$ is even with probability $\approx\frac{11}{72}$ . Hence $S_{n}$ exhibits a strong periodicity, although the Markov chain itself is aperiodic.

In the arguments of Section 5, this is reflected in the easily verified fact that $P(-1)$ has an eigenvalue $-1$ , and thus $\rho(P(-1))=1$ so Lemma 5.7 fails for $t=\pi$ . Lemma 5.7 holds for $0<t<\pi$ , and thus Lemmas 5.8 and 5.9 hold for $\delta\leqslant t\leqslant\pi-\delta$ . Furthermore, for $z$ close to $-1$ , we have in analogy with (5.11) an approximation

$$ \displaystyle G_{n}(z)=\eta_{-}(z)\lambda(z)^{n}\bigl(1+O(c^{n})\bigr) $$

with $c<1$ , where $\eta_{-}(z)$ and $\lambda(z)$ are analytic and $\lambda(-1)=-1$ ; furthermore, $\lambda(z)$ is an eigenvalue of $P(z)$ , and we have $\lambda(z)=-\lambda(-z)$ .

We can now argue as in Section 5, but we have to include terms coming from $z=-1$ . For simplicity, consider

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}=0)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\varphi_{S_{n}}(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}G_{n}(e^{\mathrm{i}t}). $$

Calculations show that $\lambda^{\prime}(1)=\lambda^{\prime}(-1)=0$ , $\lambda^{\prime\prime}(1)=\tfrac{5}{6}$ , $\lambda^{\prime\prime}(-1)=-\tfrac{5}{6}$ , $\eta(1)=1$ (as always), and $\eta(-1)=\frac{25}{36}$ ; (6.17) and standard arguments then yield

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}=0)=\frac{3}{\sqrt{5\pi n}}\Bigl(1+(-1)^{n}\frac{25}{36}+o(1)\Bigr). $$

This shows periodicity for $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}=0)$ , and in particular (3.14) does not hold. $\triangle$

### 6.2. The aperiodicity condition (3.9)

Let $L$ be the subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ generated by the set $\bigl\{(g(\mathcal{Q}),\ell(\mathcal{Q})):\mathcal{Q}\text{ is a closed path}\bigr\}$ in (3.9), and let $G:=\mathbb{Z}^{2}/L$ be the corresponding quotient. Thus the condition (3.9) says $G=\{1\}$ .

The projection $\Pi_{2}:(x,y)\mapsto y$ maps $L$ onto the subgroup $L_{2}$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ generated by the set of $\ell(\mathcal{Q})$ for all closed paths $\mathcal{Q}$ , and since we assume the aperiodicity (3.4), we have $L_{2}=\mathbb{Z}$ ; in other words, $\Pi_{2}$ is onto $\mathbb{Z}$ . Consequently, there exists some $b\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $(b,1)\in L$ . Let

$$ \displaystyle L_{1}:=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}:(x,0)\in L\}, $$

i.e., the kernel of $\Pi_{2}$ regarded as a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle(x,y)\in L\iff(x,y)-y(b,1)\in L\iff x-yb\in L_{1} $$

and thus

$$ \displaystyle L=\bigl\{(z+yb,y):y\in\mathbb{Z},z\in L_{1}\bigr\}. $$

Similarly, it follows from $(b,1)\in L$ that every coset $\overline{(x,y)}\in G$ of $L$ has a representative of the form $(z,0)$ . Consequently, the homomorphism $z\mapsto\overline{(z,0)}$ maps $\mathbb{Z}$ onto $G$ , and thus $G\cong\mathbb{Z}/L_{1}$ . Hence, $G$ is a cyclic group. Let $N:=|G|\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ . In particular, (3.9) holds if and only if $N=1$ . There are two cases:

- (i) $L_{1}=\{0\}$ , $N=\infty$ , and $G\cong\mathbb{Z}$ . Then (6.21) shows that $L=\{y(b,1):y\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ . The definition of $L$ shows that this holds if and only if $\displaystyle g(\mathcal{Q})=b\ell(\mathcal{Q})$ (6.22) for every closed path. This is a very degenerate case, see Section 6.3.

- (ii) $L_{1}=N\mathbb{Z}$ , $1\leqslant N<\infty$ , and $G\cong\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ . It follows from (6.21) that $L$ is a two-dimensional lattice with basis $\{(N,0),(b,1)\}$ .

In both cases, we identify $G$ with $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ (where $\mathbb{Z}_{\infty}:=\mathbb{Z}$ ) in the natural way by the isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/L_{1}\to G$ .

Every possible step $ij$ with $P_{ij}>0$ in the Markov chain generates a vector $v_{ij}:=(g(j),1)$ in $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , and thus a corresponding element $\gamma_{ij}:=\overline{(g(j),1)}\in G$ . If we sum $v_{ij}$ along a closed path, we get (by definition) an element of $L$ , and thus the sum of $\gamma_{ij}$ along a closed path vanishes in $G$ . Fix an (arbitrary) element $o\in\mathcal{W}$ , and pick for every $k\in\mathcal{W}$ a path $\mathcal{Q}_{k}$ from $o$ to $k$ . Let $\gamma_{k}\in G$ be the sum of $\gamma_{ij}$ along this path. It is easy to see that since the sum along any closed path is 0, the sum $\gamma_{k}$ does not depend on the choice of $\mathcal{Q}_{k}$ . Furthermore, if $P_{ij}>0$ , then we may choose $\mathcal{Q}_{j}$ as the path $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ followed by $j$ , and thus

$$ \displaystyle\gamma_{j}=\gamma_{i}+\gamma_{ij},\qquad\text{if $P_{ij}>0$}. $$

Note also that since $(b,1)\in L$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\gamma_{ij}=\overline{(g(j),1)}=\overline{(g(j)-b,0)}. $$

Hence, by identifying $G$ with $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ , we simply have $\gamma_{ij}=g(j)-b$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ , and thus by (6.23)

$$ \displaystyle\gamma_{j}=\gamma_{i}+g(j)-b\qquad\text{in $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ when $P_{ij}>0$}. $$

This leads to the following characterizations of (3.9).

#### Proposition 6.6.

Let $(W_{k})$ be an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{W}$ , and let $g:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$ . Then, with notation as in Sections 3 and 5, the following are equivalent:

- (i) The condition (3.9) does not hold.

- (ii) $P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=1$ for some $t\in(0,\pi]$ .

- (iii) The spectral radius $\rho\bigl(P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})\bigr)=1$ for some $t\in(0,\pi]$ .

- (iv) There exist an integer $N\geqslant 2$ , an integer $b$ , and integers $\gamma_{i}$ , $i\in\mathcal{W}$ , such that for every pair $i,j\in\mathcal{W}$ with $P_{ij}>0$ , $\displaystyle\gamma_{j}\equiv\gamma_{i}+g(j)-b\pmod{N}.$ (6.26)

- (v) There exists an integer $N\geqslant 2$ , an integer $b$ , and a partition of $\mathcal{W}$ into (possibly empty) sets $\mathcal{W}_{k}$ , $k=1,\dots,N$ , such that if $i\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ and $P_{ij}>0$ , then $j\in\mathcal{W}_{k+g(j)-b}$ , with the index regarded modulo $N$ .

#### Proof.

First, the proof of Lemma 5.7 shows that every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $P(e^{\mathrm{i}t})$ satisfies $|\lambda|\leqslant 1$ , and thus (ii) $\iff$ (iii) by the definition of spectral radius.

Furthermore, (iv) $\iff$ (v), since if (iv) holds, we may define $\mathcal{W}_{k}:=\{i:\gamma_{i}\equiv k\pmod{N}\}$ , and conversely we may define $\gamma_{i}=k$ for $i\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ .

Lemma 5.7 shows that if (3.9) holds, then (iii) does not hold; thus (iii) $\implies$ (i).

Now suppose that (i) holds. This means that in the discussion above, $N>1$ . If $N<\infty$ , then (6.25) shows the existence of $b$ and $\gamma_{i}$ such that (6.26) holds. If $N=\infty$ , then (6.26) holds in $\mathbb{Z}$ , and it thus holds for any integer $N\geqslant 2$ . This shows (i) $\implies$ (iv).

Finally, suppose that (iv) holds. Let $t=2\pi/N$ and $\omega:=e^{\mathrm{i}t}=e^{2\pi\mathrm{i}/N}$ , and let $v_{i}:=\omega^{-\gamma_{i}}$ . Then, by (5.5) and (6.26) if $P_{ij}>0$ , and trivially if $P_{ij}=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle P(\omega)_{ij}v_{j}=P_{ij}\omega^{g(j)-\gamma_{j}}=P_{ij}\omega^{b-g(i)}=P_{ij}\omega^{b}v_{i}, $$

and by summing over $j$ we see that $v:=(v_{i})_{i}$ is an eigenvector of $P(\omega)$ with eigenvalue $\omega^{b}$ . Hence (ii) holds. ∎

#### Example 6.7.

Nagaev [21, Condition C] makes the (rather strong) assumption that for every pair $i,j\in\mathcal{W}$ , there exists $k\in\mathcal{W}$ such that $P_{ik},P_{jk}>0$ . This in combination with (6.26) implies that

$$ \displaystyle\gamma_{i}\equiv\gamma_{k}-g(k)+b\equiv\gamma_{j}\pmod{N}. $$

Thus, for every $j$ , by choosing $i$ such that $P_{ij}>0$ and applying (6.26) again,

$$ \displaystyle g(j)\equiv b\pmod{N},\qquad j\in\mathcal{W}. $$

Since [21, Theorem 3] also assumes (in our notation) that (6.29) does not hold for any $N\geqslant 2$ , we see that the assumptions in [21] imply that Proposition 6.6(iv) cannot hold, and thus Proposition 6.6 shows that (3.9) holds. $\triangle$

### 6.3. The asymptotic variance $\sigma^{2}=0$

Another exceptional case when Theorem 1.1 fails is when the asymptotic variance $\sigma^{2}=0$ . This is a very degenerate case; as shown in Proposition 6.8 below, it happens only if, after subtracting a suitable constant $b$ from $g$ , the sums $S_{n}$ are deterministically bounded. We will also see that it cannot happen when (3.9) holds.

#### Proposition 6.8.

Let $(W_{k})$ be an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{W}$ , and let $g:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$ . Then, with notation as in Sections 3 and 6.2, the following are equivalent:

- (i) $\sigma^{2}=0$ .

- (ii) There exists an integer (or real number) $b$ such that deterministically $\displaystyle|S_{n}-bn|\leqslant C$ (6.30) for some constant $C$ , uniformly in $n$ .

- (iii) There exists an integer (or real number) $b$ such that $\displaystyle g(\mathcal{Q})=b\ell(\mathcal{Q})$ (6.31) for every closed path $\mathcal{Q}$ .

- (iv) There exist an integer $b$ and integers $\gamma_{i}$ , $i\in\mathcal{W}$ , such that for every pair $i,j\in\mathcal{W}$ with $P_{ij}>0$ , $\displaystyle\gamma_{j}=\gamma_{i}+g(j)-b.$ (6.32)

- (v) There exists an integer $b$ such that $\displaystyle L=\mathbb{Z}(b,1)=\{(yb,y):y\in\mathbb{Z}\}.$ (6.33)

- (vi) The lattice $L$ is one-dimensional.

- (vii) $L_{1}=\{0\}$ .

- (viii) $N=\infty$ .

- (ix) $G=\mathbb{Z}$ .

Furthermore, the constant $b$ in (ii), (iii), (iv), and (v) is the same integer.

#### Proof.

The equivalences (vi) $\iff$ (v) $\iff$ (vii) $\iff$ (viii) $\iff$ (ix) $\iff$ (iii) follow from the discussion at the beginning of Section 6.2, in particular (6.21) and the text leading to (6.22). Note that if (6.31) holds for some real number $b$ , then $b\ell(\mathcal{Q})\in\mathbb{Z}$ for every closed path $\mathcal{Q}$ , and thus $bx\in\mathbb{Z}$ for every $x$ in the group $L_{2}$ generated by the set of all such $\ell(\mathcal{Q})$ . As noted above, the aperiodicity (3.4) implies $L_{2}=\mathbb{Z}$ , and thus $b\in\mathbb{Z}$ , so $b$ in (6.31) has to be an integer.

Furthermore, (viii) $\implies$ (iv) follows by (6.25) (with $N=\infty$ ).

(iv) $\implies$ (ii): It follows from (6.32) that

$$ \displaystyle S_{n}-bn \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(g(W_{k})-b)=g(W_{1})-b+\sum_{k=2}^{n}(\gamma_{W_{k}}-\gamma_{W_{k-1}}) \displaystyle=g(W_{1})-b+\gamma_{W_{n}}-\gamma_{W_{1}} $$

and thus (6.30) holds with $C=\max_{i\in\mathcal{W}}|g(i)-b|+2\max_{j\in\mathcal{W}}|\gamma_{j}|$ . (The same argument yields (iv) $\implies$ (iii) directly, but we do not need this.)

(ii) $\implies$ (i): Obvious by the definition (3.12).

(i) $\implies$ (iii): Suppose that (iii) does not hold. Then there exist two closed paths $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle g(\mathcal{Q}_{1})/\ell(\mathcal{Q}_{1})\neq g(\mathcal{Q}_{2})/\ell(\mathcal{Q}_{2}). $$

Let $w_{i}$ be the starting point of $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ . If $w_{2}\neq w_{1}$ , choose two paths $\mathcal{Q}_{12}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{21}$ from $w_{1}$ to $w_{2}$ and from $w_{2}$ to $w_{1}$ , respectively. We may then construct the closed paths $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}:=\mathcal{Q}_{12}+\mathcal{Q}_{21}$ and $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}:=\mathcal{Q}_{12}+\mathcal{Q}_{2}+\mathcal{Q}_{21}$ , both starting at $w_{1}$ , by concatenation in the obvious way. Then

$$ \displaystyle g(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime})=g(\mathcal{Q}_{12})+g(\mathcal{Q}_{2})+g(\mathcal{Q}_{21})=g(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime})+g(\mathcal{Q}_{2}) $$

and similarly $\ell(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime})=\ell(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime})+\ell(\mathcal{Q}_{2})$ ; hence it follows from (6.35) that we cannot have $g(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime})/\ell(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime})=g(\mathcal{Q}_{1})/\ell(\mathcal{Q}_{1})=g(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime})/\ell(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime})$ . Consequently, by relabelling either $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ or $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime\prime}$ as $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ , we may assume that (6.35) holds with the same starting point $w_{1}$ for both closed paths.

Next, let $\ell_{i}:=\ell(\mathcal{Q}_{i})\geqslant 1$ . Replace $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ by the closed path $\ell_{3-i}\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ , i.e., the closed path $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ repeated $\ell_{3-i}$ times. This replacement does not change $g(\mathcal{Q}_{i})/\ell(\mathcal{Q}_{i})$ , and thus (6.35) still holds, but now both closed paths have the same length $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}$ .

We may thus assume that (6.35) holds for two closed paths $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ of the same length $\ell\geqslant 1$ and starting from the same point $w_{1}\in\mathcal{W}$ ; note that this implies $g(\mathcal{Q}_{1})\neq g(\mathcal{Q}_{2})$ . We now fix these paths, and thus $\ell$ , and define a sequence of stopping times for the Markov chain by

$$ \displaystyle T_{0} \displaystyle:=\min\{n\geqslant 1:W_{n}=w_{1}\}, \displaystyle T_{k} \displaystyle:=\min\{n\geqslant T_{k-1}+\ell:W_{n}=w_{1}\},\qquad k\geqslant 1. $$

Thus, at $T_{k}$ we return to $w_{1}$ , but we only consider returns after a time of at least $\ell$ .

Since the Markov chain is finite and irreducible, almost surely all $T_{k}$ are finite. The Markov property shows that the times $T_{k}$ are renewal times in the sense that the process starts again at each $T_{k}$ . Let $\tau_{k}:=T_{k}-T_{k-1}$ , the waiting time of the $k$ :th “renewal”; then $\tau_{1}$ , $\tau_{2}$ , …are i.i.d. random variables. Using the fact that there exists some $t_{0}$ such that from every point in $\mathcal{W}$ we may with positive probability reach $w_{1}$ within $t_{0}$ steps, it is easily seen that the tail probability $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(\tau_{1}>t)$ decreases exponentially as $t\to\infty$ ; in particular, the moment $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}\tau_{1}^{m}$ is finite for every $m\geqslant 1$ , Similarly, $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}T_{0}^{m}<\infty$ .

Consider the two-dimensional process $(n,S_{n})$ and its “increments” between the renewal times $T_{k}$ defined by

$$ \displaystyle\zeta_{k}:=\bigl(T_{k}-T_{k-1},\{S_{T_{k-1}+i}-S_{T_{k-1}}:0\leqslant i\leqslant T_{k}-T_{k-1}\}\bigr),\qquad k\geqslant 1, $$

where the second component thus is a random process defined on an integer interval of random length. The Markov property shows that these increments are i.i.d. We may thus apply the general result from renewal theory stated in Lemma 6.9 below and conclude that, with the notation in (6.42)–(6.44), (6.45) holds with convergence of all moments. In particular,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\operatorname{Var}[S_{n}]}{n}=\operatorname{Var}\Bigl(\frac{S_{n}-an}{\sqrt{n}}\Bigr)\to\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}/\widetilde{\mu} $$

and thus, recalling (3.12),

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}=\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}/\widetilde{\mu}. $$

Now recall the closed paths $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ of the same length $\ell$ constructed above. For each $i=1,2$ , with positive probability the Markov chain starts in $w_{1}$ and then follows $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ for the next $\ell$ steps; in this case $T_{0}=1$ and $T_{1}=\ell+1$ so $\tau_{1}=\ell$ , and also $S_{T_{1}}-S_{T_{0}}=g(\mathcal{Q}_{i})$ . Consequently, $S_{T_{1}}-S_{T_{0}}-aT_{1}$ takes two different values $g(\mathcal{Q}_{i})-a\ell$ with positive probability, and thus $\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}>0$ by (6.44) and consequently $\sigma^{2}>0$ by (6.41), so (i) does not hold. This completes the proof of (i) $\implies$ (iii), which completes the chain of equivalences. ∎

We used above the following renewal theoretic lemma, stated here for our Markov chain and $S_{n}$ . The lemma follows easily from known general results in renewal theory; we find it convenient to use a version from [15] that uses a formulation from [28]. The powerful idea to analyze Markov chains (also with an infinite state space) by a suitable renewal sequence of stopping times is old, and was for example used by [12].

#### Lemma 6.9.

Let $(T_{k})_{k=0}^{\infty}$ be an increasing sequence of (a.s. finite) random times and let $\tau_{k}:=T_{k}-T_{k-1}$ , $k\geqslant 1$ . Assume that the increments $\zeta_{k}$ defined in (6.39) for $k\geqslant 1$ are i.i.d. (Thus, in particular, the increments $\tau_{k}$ are i.i.d.) Assume also that for every $r\geqslant 1$ , $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}T_{0}^{r}<\infty$ and $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}\tau_{1}^{r}<\infty$ . Let

$$ \displaystyle a \displaystyle:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[S_{T_{1}}-S_{T_{0}}]/\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[\tau_{1}], \displaystyle\widetilde{\mu} \displaystyle:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}[\tau_{1}], \displaystyle\widetilde{\sigma}^{2} \displaystyle:=\operatorname{Var}[S_{T_{1}}-S_{T_{0}}-a\tau_{1}]. $$

Then, as ${n\to\infty}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{S_{n}-an}{\sqrt{n}}\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\longrightarrow}N\bigl(0,\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}/\widetilde{\mu}\bigr) $$

with convergence of all moments.

#### Proof.

Consider first the process only from time $T_{0}$ . Formally we define

$$ \displaystyle S_{n}^{\prime}:=S_{T_{0}+n}-S_{T_{0}} $$

and note that $(S_{n}^{\prime})_{n=0}^{\infty}$ is a stochastic process that starts at time $n=0$ with $S^{\prime}_{0}=0$ ; define also $T_{n}^{\prime}:=T_{n}-T_{0}$ . Then the increments $\zeta_{k}$ in (6.39) are the same for $(S_{n}^{\prime})$ and $(T_{k}^{\prime})$ as for $(S_{n})$ and $(T_{k})$ . By assumption these are i.i.d.; this means that in the terminology of [28] and [15], the stochastic process $S_{n}^{\prime}$ has regenerative increments over the times $T^{\prime}_{k}$ .

Since the state space $\mathcal{W}$ is finite, the function $g$ is bounded, and thus $|S^{\prime}_{T_{1}}|\leqslant C(T_{1}-T_{0})=C\tau_{1}$ ; consequently the moment $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}|S^{\prime}_{T_{1}}|^{r}$ is finite for every $r\geqslant 1$ . Moreover, if $M_{1}:=\sup_{1\leqslant n\leqslant T^{\prime}_{1}}|S^{\prime}_{n}|$ then $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}M_{1}^{r}<\infty$ by the same argument.

We may now apply [15, Theorems 1.4 and 3.1] and conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{S^{\prime}_{n}-an}{\sqrt{n}}\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\longrightarrow}N\bigl(0,\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}/\widetilde{\mu}\bigr) $$

with convergence of all moments.

Finally, again since $g$ is bounded, $|S_{T_{0}+n}-S_{n}|\leqslant CT_{0}$ and $|S_{T_{0}}|\leqslant CT_{0}$ , and consequently

$$ \displaystyle|S_{n}-S_{n}^{\prime}|\leqslant|S_{T_{0}+n}-S_{n}|+|S_{T_{0}}|\leqslant CT_{0}. $$

It follows that, as ${n\to\infty}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{S_{n}-S_{n}^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}\to 0 $$

in probability, which together with (6.47) implies (6.45). Moreover, since $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}T_{0}^{p}<\infty$ for every $p\geqslant 1$ , it follows from (6.48) that (6.49) holds in $L^{p}$ for every $p\geqslant 1$ , which together with the moment convergence in (6.47) implies that all moments converge in (6.45) too. ∎

#### Corollary 6.10.

Let $(W_{k})$ be an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{W}$ , and let $g:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$ . Then, with notation as in Sections 3, if (3.9) holds, then $\sigma^{2}>0$ .

#### Proof.

Proposition 6.8 shows that if $\sigma^{2}=0$ , then (6.31) holds and thus (3.9) does not hold. ∎

This corollary completes the proof of Theorem 3.2.

## 7. Back to Litt’s game

We consider again Litt’s game. We begin by showing that the only cases where $\sigma^{2}=0$ are the rather trivial cases in Example 6.2 (including Example 6.1). This (in the form (7.1) below) is stated in Basdevant et al. [1] without proof; since we also do not know of a proof given elsewhere, we give a complete proof.

#### Theorem 7.1.

For Litt’s game in Section 4, we have $\sigma^{2}>0$ except in the case $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}\mathsf{H}$ (with $q=2$ and some $\ell\geqslant 2$ ) and its variants obtained by interchanging Alice and Bob or $\mathsf{H}$ and $\mathsf{T}$ (or both).

#### Proof.

Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are distinct words such that $\sigma^{2}=0$ . By (4.19), this is equivalent to

$$ \displaystyle 1+\theta_{AA}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}+\theta_{BB}=0. $$

Note first that for any two words $U$ and $V$ of length $\ell$ , (4.10) yields

$$ \displaystyle 0\leqslant\theta_{UV}\leqslant\sum_{k=1}^{\ell-1}q^{k-\ell}=\frac{1-q^{-(\ell-1)}}{q-1}<\frac{1}{q-1}. $$

Hence, (7.1) is impossible if $q\geqslant 3$ , and thus we in the rest of the proof assume $q=2$ and take the alphabet to be $\{\mathsf{H},\mathsf{T}\}$ . Furthermore, we have to have $\ell\geqslant 2$ , since $\theta_{UV}=0$ when $\ell=1$ .

Moreover, if $\ell-1\notin\Theta(U,V)$ , then similarly

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{UV}\leqslant\sum_{k=1}^{\ell-2}2^{k-\ell}<\frac{1}{2}. $$

Hence, (7.1) cannot hold unless $\ell-1\in\Theta(A,B)$ or $\ell-1\in\Theta(B,A)$ . By symmetry, we may assume the first, i.e., that the last $\ell-1$ letters in $A$ are the same as the first $\ell-1$ letters in $B$ . By symmetry, we may also assume that $A$ ends with $\mathsf{T}$ . This means that for some word $C$ of length $\ell-2$ and some letters $a,b\in\{\mathsf{H},\mathsf{T}\}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle A \displaystyle=aC\mathsf{T},\qquad B=C\mathsf{T}b. $$

Recall from Section 4 that $\widehat{S}_{n}=S_{n-\ell+1}=\sum_{k=1}^{n-\ell-1}g(\xi_{k}\dotsm\xi_{k+\ell-1})$ where $g:\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{Z}$ is given by $g=I_{A}-I_{B}$ ; thus

$$ \displaystyle g(A)=1,\quad g(B)=-1,\quad\text{and otherwise }g=0. $$

We use [14, Theorem 2] which shows that then the asymptotic variance $\sigma^{2}=0$ if and only if there exists a function $h:\mathcal{A}^{\ell-1}\to\mathbb{R}$ and a constant $\mu$ such that for any word $a_{1}\dotsm a_{\ell}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle g(a_{1}\dotsm a_{\ell})=h(a_{2}\dotsm a_{\ell})-h(a_{1}\dotsm a_{\ell-1})+\mu. $$

(In fact, it follows from (7.6) that $\mu=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}g(\xi_{1}\dotsm\xi_{\ell})=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}g(W_{1})=0$ , and thus $\mu=0$ is the same as before, see (4.8).)

We have $A=aC\mathsf{T}$ by (7.4), and thus $aC\mathsf{H}\neq A$ . Hence, (7.5) and (7.6) yield

$$ \displaystyle 0<g(aC\mathsf{T})-g(aC\mathsf{H})=h(C\mathsf{T})-h(C\mathsf{H}). $$

Let $\bar{a}$ be the letter in $\{\mathsf{H},\mathsf{T}\}$ distinct from $a$ . Then by (7.6) again and (7.7),

$$ \displaystyle g(\bar{a}C\mathsf{T})-g(\bar{a}C\mathsf{H})=h(C\mathsf{T})-h(C\mathsf{H})>0. $$

Since $\bar{a}C\mathsf{T}\neq A$ , (7.8) is possible only if $\bar{a}C\mathsf{H}=B$ . Thus, by (7.4),

$$ \displaystyle\bar{a}C\mathsf{H}=B=C\mathsf{T}b. $$

Hence, $b=\mathsf{H}$ and

$$ \displaystyle\bar{a}C=C\mathsf{T}. $$

By counting the number of $\mathsf{T}$ s on both sides, we see that $\bar{a}=\mathsf{T}$ , and thus $a=\mathsf{H}$ . Finally, (7.10) shows that $C\mathsf{T}$ is invariant under cyclic permutations, and thus must contain only one letter; hence $C=\mathsf{T}^{\ell-2}$ . The conclusion $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}\mathsf{H}$ now follows from (7.4). ∎

### 7.1. The aperiodicity condition for Litt’s game

We next show that for Litt’s game, also the aperiodicity condition (3.9) is satisfied except in the (more or less trivial) cases in Examples 6.2, 6.4 and 6.3, i.e., in the exceptional cases in Theorem 7.1 and also in the cases $(\mathsf{H},\mathsf{T})$ and $(\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H},\mathsf{T}\mathsf{T})$ (or vice versa).

#### Theorem 7.2.

For Litt’s game in Section 4, the aperiodicity condition (3.9) holds except in the cases (all with $q=2$ )

- (i) $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}^{\ell-1}\mathsf{H}$ for some $\ell\geqslant 2$ (see Example 6.2),

- (ii) $A=\mathsf{H}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}$ (see Example 6.3),

- (iii) $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}\mathsf{T}$ (see Example 6.4),

and their variants obtained by interchanging Alice and Bob or $\mathsf{H}$ and $\mathsf{T}$ (or both).

#### Proof.

Recall that a path $\mathcal{Q}$ is a sequence $i_{0},\dots,i_{m}$ in $\mathcal{W}=\mathcal{A}^{\ell}$ , with each transition having a positive probability. The length is defined as $m$ and the value $g(\mathcal{Q})$ is $\sum_{k=1}^{m}g(i_{k})$ . Define the weight of the path as $w(\mathcal{Q}):=\prod_{k=1}^{m}P_{i_{k-1},i_{k}}$ ; this is the probability that if the Markov chain starts in $i_{0}$ , it will follow $\mathcal{Q}$ for the next $m$ steps.

To satisfy the aperiodicity condition, it is sufficient to show:

- (a) There exists a closed path $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ such that $g(\mathcal{Q}_{1})=0$ and $\ell(\mathcal{Q}_{1})=1$ .

- (b) There exists a closed path $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ such that $g(\mathcal{Q}_{2})=1$ .

In this case, there exists some $N\geqslant 1$ such that $(0,1)$ and $(1,N)$ are in the set $\bigl\{(g(\mathcal{Q}),\ell(\mathcal{Q})):\mathcal{Q}\text{ is a closed path}\bigr\}$ in (3.9) and it is clear that these two vectors together generate $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ ; thus (3.9) holds.

The first condition (a) is simple, since for every $a\in\mathcal{A}$ , $a\cdots a\to a\cdots a$ is a closed path in $\mathcal{W}$ of length 1. If $q\geqslant 3$ , or $q=2$ and at least one of $A$ or $B$ is non-constant, then at least one of these paths also has value 0, thus satisfying (a). The remaining case $q=2$ with $A=\mathsf{H}^{\ell}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}^{\ell}$ (or vice versa) is as noted an exception if $\ell\leqslant 2$ ; if $\ell\geqslant 3$ , (a) does not hold but we note that the sequences of coin tosses obtained by repeating $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}$ or $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}$ yields closed paths $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{3}$ with lengths 2 and 3 and value 0, which is just as good since $\gcd(2,3)=1$ .

To show (b), it is sufficient to show there exists a closed path through $A$ (of length $\geqslant 1$ ) that avoids $B$ . Given such a path, we can truncate it to the time of first return to $A$ to ensure that the value of the path is $1$ .

Let $W(m)$ be the total weight of all closed paths from $A$ with length $m$ , that avoid $B$ , with $W(0):=1$ . It is easily seen that these numbers have the following generating function:

$$ \displaystyle(I-tP_{\neq B})^{-1}_{A,A}=\sum_{m\geqslant 0}W(m)t^{m} $$

where $P_{\neq B}$ is given by zero-ing out the column of $P$ corresponding to $B$ .

We need to show that at least one $W(m)$ is non-zero for $m>0$ . We will do this by showing that $\sum_{m\geqslant 0}W(m)>W(0)=1$ . For this we use the formula (7.16) in Lemma 7.3 below, which together with (7.11) gives

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m\geqslant 0}W(m)=(I-P_{\neq B})^{-1}_{A,A}=Q_{AA}+Q_{BB}-Q_{AB}-Q_{BA}. $$

(An alternative proof of (7.12) is given in Appendix B.) The explicit formula (4.27) now yields

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m\geqslant 0}W(m)=2+\theta_{AA}+\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}. $$

Hence, by (7.13) and (4.19),

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m\geqslant 0}W(m)>1\iff 1+\theta_{AA}+\theta_{BB}-\theta_{AB}-\theta_{BA}>0\iff\sigma^{2}>0, $$

which holds by Theorem 7.1 except in the excluded case (i). ∎

The proof above used the following lemma. (See also Appendix B.)

#### Lemma 7.3.

Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on a finite state space $\mathcal{W}$ , and let $\pi$ be its stationary distribution. Then, for any $B\in\mathcal{W}$ , the matrix $(I-P_{\neq B})$ is invertible, and the inverse has the entries, for $i,j\in\mathcal{W}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(I-P_{\neq B})_{ij}^{-1}=Q_{ij}+\bigl(Q_{BB}+(I-Q)_{iB}\bigr)\frac{\pi_{j}}{\pi_{B}}-Q_{Bj}. $$

In particular, if the stationary distribution $\pi$ is uniform, then

$$ \displaystyle(I-P_{\neq B})_{ij}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{1}_{i=B}+Q_{ij}+Q_{BB}-Q_{iB}-Q_{Bj}. $$

#### Proof.

Recall the identity $(I-P)Q=I-\textbf{1}\pi^{t}$ (2.19). Hence, $PQ=Q-I+\textbf{1}\pi^{t}$ . Thus, using the Kronecker delta $\delta_{kj}:=\boldsymbol{1}_{k=j}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(P_{\neq B}Q)_{kj} \displaystyle=\sum_{i\neq B}P_{ki}Q_{ij} \displaystyle=(PQ)_{kj}-P_{kB}Q_{Bj} \displaystyle=Q_{kj}-\delta_{kj}-\pi_{j}-P_{kB}Q_{Bj}. $$

Similarly

$$ \displaystyle\smash{\sum_{i}}(P_{\neq B})_{ki}(I-Q)_{iB} \displaystyle=(P(I-Q))_{kB}-P_{kB}(I-Q)_{BB} \displaystyle=P_{kB}+(I-Q-\textbf{1}\pi^{t})_{kB}-P_{kB}(1-Q_{BB}) \displaystyle=P_{kB}+\delta_{kB}-Q_{kB}-\pi_{B}-P_{kB}+Q_{BB}P_{kB} \displaystyle=\delta_{kB}-Q_{kB}-\pi_{B}+Q_{BB}P_{kB} $$

So if we define $M_{ij}$ to be the right hand side of (7.15), then, using $\sum_{i\neq B}P_{ki}=1-P_{kB}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(P_{\neq B}M)_{kj} \displaystyle=\sum_{i}(P_{\neq B})_{ki}\left(Q_{ij}+\left(Q_{BB}+(I-Q)_{iB}\right){\frac{\pi_{j}}{\pi_{B}}}-Q_{Bj}\right) \displaystyle=Q_{kj}-\delta_{kj}+\pi_{j}-P_{kB}Q_{Bj}+\bigl((1-P_{kB})Q_{BB} \displaystyle\qquad+\delta_{kB}-Q_{kB}-\pi_{B}+Q_{BB}P_{kB}\bigr){\frac{\pi_{j}}{\pi_{B}}}-(1-P_{kB})Q_{Bj} \displaystyle=-\delta_{kj}+Q_{kj}+\pi_{j}-P_{kB}Q_{Bj}+\left(Q_{BB}+\delta_{kB}-Q_{kB}\right){\frac{\pi_{j}}{\pi_{B}}} \displaystyle\qquad-\pi_{j}-Q_{Bj}+P_{kB}Q_{Bj} \displaystyle=-\delta_{kj}+Q_{kj}+\left(Q_{BB}+(I-Q)_{kB}\right){\frac{\pi_{j}}{\pi_{B}}}-Q_{Bj} \displaystyle=-\delta_{kj}+M_{kj}. $$

Thus $(I-P_{\neq B})M=I$ and the claim follows. ∎

#### Remark 7.4.

An alternative proof of this lemma proceeds by writing $I-P_{\neq B}=I-P+uv^{t}=(I-P+\textbf{1}\pi^{t})+(uv^{t}-\textbf{1}\pi^{t})$ for appropriate vectors $u,v$ . Since the matrix $I-P+\textbf{1}\pi^{t}$ is invertible (Proposition 2.1), we can now apply the standard Woodbury formula to write $(I-P_{\neq B})^{-1}$ as a rank-2 correction to $(I-P+\textbf{1}\pi^{t})^{-1}=Q+\textbf{1}\pi^{t}$ . A similar argument also works to derive a general formula for rank- $k$ updates to $I-P$ . The details are straightforward and left to the reader. $\triangle$

#### Remark 7.5.

The quantity $\sum_{m\geqslant 0}W(m)=(I-P_{\neq B})_{AA}^{-1}$ has the alternative probablistic interpretation the expected number of visits to $A$ before visiting $B$ for a Markov chain started at $A$ (counting the initial state as a visit). This follows by considering $N_{i}$ , the expected number of visits to $A$ before visiting $B$ for a random walk started at $i$ , and observing the linear relation $N_{i}=\textbf{1}_{i=A}+\sum_{j\neq B}P_{ij}N_{j}$ . $\triangle$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

By Theorem 7.2, except in the excluded cases and in the case $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}\mathsf{T}$ (or conversely), the condition (3.9) holds and then the result is given by Theorem 4.2.

In the remaining case $A=\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}$ and $B=\mathsf{T}\mathsf{T}$ , (3.9) fails but $\sigma^{2}>0$ and (1.5)–(1.8) still hold by simple direct calculations, see Example 6.4. ∎

## 8. Analysis of state space expansion

The proof of Theorem 3.4 involves passing to the expanded state space of pairs $(i,j)$ . In order to modify the explicit moment formulas for this case, it is necessary to know how the stationary distribution $\pi$ and group inverse $Q$ are transformed under this state-space-expansion operation.

The expanded transition matrix $\widehat{P}_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}$ evidently satisfies

$$ \widehat{P}_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}=\boldsymbol{1}_{j=i^{\prime}}P_{j,j^{\prime}} $$

We have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{ij}\pi_{i}P_{i,j}\widehat{P}_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\sum_{ij}\pi_{i}P_{i,j}\boldsymbol{1}_{j=i^{\prime}}P_{j,j^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\sum_{i}\pi_{i}P_{i,i^{\prime}}P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\pi_{i^{\prime}}P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}} $$

Therefore the expanded stationary distribution is

$$ \Pi_{ij}=\pi_{i}P_{ij} $$

We also need to work out the expanded group inverse $\widehat{Q}:=(I-\widehat{P})^{\mathsf{g}}$ . A simple induction shows

$$ \displaystyle(\widehat{P}^{k})_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle(P^{k-1})_{j,i^{\prime}}P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}} $$

for $k\geqslant 1$ . Another way to see this is to note that a length- $k$ path in the extended state space from $(i,j)$ to $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})$ can be decomposed into a length $k-1$ path in the original state spce between $j$ and $i^{\prime}$ , together with the transition $i^{\prime}\to j$ .

Therefore, for $0\leqslant t<1$ :

$$ \displaystyle(I-t\widehat{P})_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{-1} \displaystyle=I_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}+\sum_{k\geqslant 1}t^{k}(\widehat{P}^{k})_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}} \displaystyle=I_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}+\sum_{k\geqslant 1}t^{k}(P^{k-1})_{j,i^{\prime}}P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}} \displaystyle=I_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}+P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}t\sum_{k\geqslant 0}t^{k}(P^{k})_{j,i^{\prime}} \displaystyle=I_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}+P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}t(I-tP)^{-1}_{j,i^{\prime}}. $$

Using the group inverse formula in Proposition 2.1 and (8.3) thus yields:

$$ \displaystyle(I-\widehat{P})_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{g}} \displaystyle=\lim_{t\nearrow 1}\bigl((I-t\widehat{P})_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{-1}-\pi_{i^{\prime}}P_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}/(1-t)\bigr) \displaystyle=\lim_{t\nearrow 1}\bigl(\boldsymbol{1}_{i=i^{\prime},j=j^{\prime}}+tP_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(I-tP)_{j,i^{\prime}}^{-1}-\pi_{i^{\prime}}P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}/(1-t)\bigr) \displaystyle=\boldsymbol{1}_{i=i^{\prime},j=j^{\prime}}+P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}\lim_{t\nearrow 1}\left(t(I-tP)_{j,i^{\prime}}^{-1}-\pi_{i^{\prime}}/(1-t)\right). $$

Now:

$$ \displaystyle t(I-tP)^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}/(1-t) \displaystyle= \displaystyle t(I-tP)^{-1}-t\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}/(1-t)+(-1+t)\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}/(1-t) \displaystyle= \displaystyle t\bigl((I-tP)^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}/(1-t)\bigr)-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}. $$

Thus, using Proposition 2.1 again,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\nearrow 1}\bigl(t(I-tP)^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}/(1-t)\bigr)=(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}-\boldsymbol{1}\pi^{\mathsf{t}}. $$

Returning to the previous calculation in (8.6), we thus find by (8.8)

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{Q}_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}=(I-\widehat{P})^{\mathsf{g}}_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\boldsymbol{1}_{i=i^{\prime},j=j^{\prime}}+P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(Q_{j,i^{\prime}}-\pi_{i^{\prime}}), $$

where $Q=(I-P)^{\mathsf{g}}$ as before. Consequently, $\widehat{Q}^{\prime}:=\widehat{Q}-I$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{Q}^{\prime}_{ij,i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}=P_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(Q_{j,i^{\prime}}-\pi_{i^{\prime}}), $$

Now we can directly apply the explicit moment formulas (3.15)–(3.19) to the expanded state space.

## 9. Further remarks

### 9.1. Some extensions

We give here some rather brief comments on extensions of the basic Theorems 3.2 and 3.4 for finite-state Markov chains. We discuss three such extensions separately; they may without difficulty be combined.

#### 9.1.1. Higher order expansions

We have in our results only considered one-term Edgeworth expansions, with an extra term of order $n^{-1/2}$ and error of order $O(n^{-1})$ . It is by the methods above possible to obtain also expansions with further terms and errors of order $n^{-m/2}$ for, in principle, any integer $m$ . This is achieved by taking the Taylor expansion in (5.39) to higher order, and then arguing as above and in [6]. Note, however, that then also $\gamma(t)$ has to be expanded explicitly in (5.39), and thus the higher order terms in the expansion will also depend on the first derivatives $\lambda^{(m)}(1)$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda(z)$ at $z=1$ . These derivatives can be found e.g. by repeatedly differentiating the characteristic equation

$$ \displaystyle\det\bigl(P(z)-\lambda(z)I\bigr)=0 $$

at $z=1$ . We leave the details to the reader. See also [5] for asymptotic expansions with higher order terms for the original $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}$ vs $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}$ problem.

#### 9.1.2. Arbitrary initial values

One generalization of Theorem 3.2 is to add to $S_{n}$ some initial value, say $h(X_{1})$ for a given function $h:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$ ; thus now

$$ \displaystyle S_{n}:=h(X_{1})+\sum_{k=1}^{n}g(W_{k}). $$

An example where this occurs is if Alice and Bob score words of different lengths. For a simple example, suppose that Alice scores a point when $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}$ appears, while Bob scores a point when $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}$ or $\mathsf{T}\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}$ appears. From the third coinflip on, this is exactly the original problem in disguise, but here Alice may also gain a point when the second coin is tossed. If we as in Section 4 consider the Markov chain consisting of $W_{k}$ given by (4.2), now taking $\ell=3$ , then the net score is $S_{n-2}$ given by (9.2) with a suitable $g$ and $h:=I_{\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}}+I_{\mathsf{H}\mathsf{H}\mathsf{T}}$ .

In this version, Lemmas 5.2–5.4 still hold, provided we replace $\pi_{1}(z)$ defined in (5.6) by

$$ \displaystyle\pi^{h}_{1}(z)=(\pi^{h}_{1}(z)_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{W}}\quad\text{where}\quad\pi^{h}_{1}(z)_{i}:=\pi_{1;i}z^{g(i)+h(i)}. $$

However, this modification changes also $\eta(z)$ by (5.25), and since $\gamma^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{i}\eta^{\prime}(1)$ by (5.28), $\gamma^{\prime}(0)$ may be modified and is in general no longer 0, so Corollary 5.5 does not hold. In fact, by taking derivatives in (5.25) and comparing with the original case with $h=0$ (for which $\eta^{\prime}(1)=\gamma^{\prime}(0)=0$ by the proof in Section 5), we see that

$$ \displaystyle\eta^{\prime}(1)=0+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{W}}\pi_{1;j}h(j)=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}h(W_{1}), $$

and hence,

$$ \displaystyle\gamma^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{i}\eta^{\prime}(1)=\mathrm{i}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}h(W_{1}). $$

If we still let $\mu:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X_{k}$ , and also

$$ \displaystyle\Delta:=-\mathrm{i}\gamma^{\prime}(0)=\eta^{\prime}(1)=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}h(W_{1}), $$

then obviously

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}S_{n}=n\mu+\Delta. $$

In particular, Lemma 5.4 implies $\varkappa_{1}=\mu$ .

It is now necessary to include a term $\gamma^{\prime}(0)t=\mathrm{i}\Delta t$ in the Taylor expansion (5.39). The rest of the proof goes through if we replace $n\mu$ by $n\mu+\Delta$ , and thus (3.14) holds with this change. We may then replace $x$ by $x-\Delta/(\sigma\sqrt{n})$ , which using Taylor expansions yields

$$ \operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}-n\mu\leqslant x\sigma\sqrt{n})=\Phi(x)+\frac{\varkappa_{3}}{6\sigma^{3}\sqrt{2\pi n}}(1-x^{2})e^{-x^{2}/2}-\frac{\Delta}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n}}e^{-x^{2}/2}\\
+\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n}}\vartheta(x\sigma\sqrt{n}-n\mu)e^{-x^{2}/2}+O\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr). $$

In other words, (3.14) holds with an extra term $-\Delta/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n})e^{-x^{2}/2}$ . We omit the details. In Corollary 3.3, this means an extra term $-\Delta/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n})$ in (3.20) and (3.21), and thus twice as much in (3.22).

This should not be surprising. Consider for simplicity the case $\mu=0$ and $x=0$ in Corollary 3.3. If $h(W):=1$ deterministically, so we just add 1 to $S_{n}$ , then $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}\leqslant 0)$ is decreased by $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}=0)$ , which up to $O(1/n)$ equals $1/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi n})$ by (3.23). Hence the result just shown says that if (9.2) holds so the score on the average is increased by $\Delta=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}h(W_{1})$ compared to the standard case, then the probability $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}{}}(S_{n}\leqslant 0)$ shifts by $\Delta$ times as much as if we instead add 1 deterministically.

#### 9.1.3. Arbitrary initial distribution

We have asssumed in Theorems 3.2 and 3.4 that the Markov chain is stationary. We may generalize to an arbitrary initial distribution $\pi_{1}$ (or, in Theorem 3.4, $\pi_{0}$ ). Then Lemmas 5.2–5.4 still hold, with $\lambda(z)$ still given by (5.25). However, as in Section 9.1.2, in general $\gamma^{\prime}(0)\neq 0$ , so Corollary 5.5 does not hold. (We still have $\gamma^{\prime}(0)=\mathrm{i}\eta^{\prime}(1)$ by (5.28), and $\eta(z)$ depends on $\pi_{1}$ by (5.24).) If we define $\mu:=\varkappa_{1}$ , then Lemma 5.4 shows that $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}S_{n}/n=\kappa_{1}(S_{n})/n\to\mu$ , but in general $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}S_{n}$ is not equal to $n\mu$ ; in fact, (5.33) with $m=1$ implies that

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}S_{n}-n\mu=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}X_{k}-\mu)\to\Delta:=-\mathrm{i}\gamma^{\prime}(0). $$

As in Section 9.1.2, it is now necessary to include a term $\gamma^{\prime}(0)t=\mathrm{i}\Delta t$ in the Taylor expansion (5.39). This has the same consequences as in Section 9.1.2, and again we have (9.8) and its consequences.

Again this is not surprising: a different initial distribution implies by (9.9) an average extra score $\Delta$ , and (up to order $n^{-1}$ ) the probabilities in Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 shift by an amount proportional to this average extra score, just as in Section 9.1.2.

### 9.2. Litt’s game with several words each

We observe that our result Theorem 3.2 can be applied to an even more general formulation of Litt’s game, in which Alice and Bob each have several words that yield positive points for them (this generalization is considered by [5]); moreover, we may let different words give different numbers of points. As before, the value of each word is encoded in the function $g$ (with a $\pm$ sign depending on whether it gives points to Alice or Bob).

If we can verify (3.9) holds for the chain so defined, then Theorem 3.2 applies; combining (3.15)–(3.19) with Proposition 4.1 gives explicit formulas for the asymptotics directly analogous with the two-word case (although the formulas do not simplify as much in the general case). Verifying (3.9) in this case is however more difficult, since we do not have an analogue of Theorem 7.2. However we can often verify (3.9) on a case-by-case basis by an adaptation of the proof of Theorem 7.2. For example, if neither Alice nor Bob gets points for $\mathsf{H}\dotsm\mathsf{H}$ , and furthermore $[z]\operatorname{Tr}(I-P(z))^{-1}>0$ , then (3.9) holds (and hence everything goes through as in the two-word case). In general, it is an interesting question to what extent we can characterize the conditions under which (3.9) holds in the multiple-word case.

## Appendix A Taylor expansion of eigenvalues

We give here a direct proof of the Taylor expansion (5.61)–(5.64) of the eigenvalue $\lambda(F(t))$ . Both the result and the method are old, but we do not know an explicit reference so we give the details here for completeness. It is obvious that the calculations can be continued to the derivative of an arbitrary order, but we need only the first three derivatives.

#### Proposition A.1.

Let $t\mapsto F(t)$ be a $C^{3}$ (three times continuously differentiable) map defined on some neighborhood of $0$ and with values $F(t)$ in the space of $m\times m$ matrices for some $m\geqslant 1$ . Suppose that $F(0)$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda_{0}$ that is (algebraically) simple. Let $Q$ be the group inverse of $\lambda_{0}I-F(0)$ and let $u^{\mathsf{t}}$ and $v$ be left and right eigenvectors of $F(0)$ for the eigenvalue $0$ , with the normalization $u^{\mathsf{t}}v=1$ . (Such vectors exist since the eigenvalue is simple.) Then, for $t$ in a possibly smaller neighborhood of $0$ , $F(t)$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda(t)$ such that $\lambda(0)=\lambda_{0}$ and $t\mapsto\lambda(t)$ is $C^{3}$ with, writing $F^{\prime},F^{\prime\prime},F^{\prime\prime\prime}$ for $F^{\prime}(0),F^{\prime\prime}(0),F^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{\prime}(0) \displaystyle=u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}v, \displaystyle\lambda^{\prime\prime}(0) \displaystyle=u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime}v+2u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}QF^{\prime}v. \displaystyle\lambda^{\prime\prime\prime}(0) \displaystyle=u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime\prime}v+3u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime}QF^{\prime}v+3u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}QF^{\prime\prime}v+6u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}QF^{\prime}QF^{\prime}v \displaystyle\qquad-6(u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}v)(u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}Q^{2}F^{\prime}v). $$

#### Proof.

By replacing $F(t)$ by $F(t)-\lambda_{0}I$ we may assume that $\lambda_{0}=0$ . Then $Q$ is the group inverse of $-F(0)$ . (Sorry for the minus sign with our choice of notation!)

The characteristic polynomial $f(\lambda;t):=\det(\lambda I-F(t))$ has coefficients that are $C^{3}$ , and $\lambda_{0}=0$ is a simple root of $f(\cdot;0)$ ; thus $f(0,0)=0$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial\lambda}(0,0)\neq 0$ . Hence the implicit function theorem shows the existence of a $C^{3}$ function $\lambda(t)$ that is a simple root of $f(t)$ , and thus a simple eigenvalue of $F(t)$ , with $\lambda(0)=0$ . It remains only to compute the derivatives at 0.

It follows, e.g. using Cramer’s rule, that for small $t$ there exists an eigenvector $v(t)$ of $F(t)$ such that $v(t)$ is a $C^{3}$ function of $t$ with

$$ \displaystyle v(0) \displaystyle=v, \displaystyle F(t)v(t) \displaystyle=\lambda(t)v(t), \displaystyle u^{\mathsf{t}}v(t) \displaystyle=1. $$

We now differentiate the eigenvalue equation (A.5), which yields

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{\prime}(t)v(t)+\lambda(t)v^{\prime}(t)=F^{\prime}(t)v(t)+F(t)v^{\prime}(t). $$

Multiply to the left by $u^{\mathsf{t}}$ , and note that repeated differentiating of (A.6) yields

$$ \displaystyle u^{\mathsf{t}}v^{(k)}(t)=0,\qquad k\geqslant 1. $$

Hence, (A.7) yields, using (A.6) and (A.8),

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{\prime}(t)=u^{\mathsf{t}}\bigl(\lambda^{\prime}(t)v(t)+\lambda(t)v^{\prime}(t)\bigr)=u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(t)v(t)+u^{\mathsf{t}}F(t)v^{\prime}(t). $$

Taking $t=0$ and recalling $u^{\mathsf{t}}F(0)=0$ we obtain (A.1).

Since $Q$ is the group inverse of $-F(0)$ , and $F(0)v=0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle Qv=0. $$

Moreover, (A.8) shows that $v^{\prime}(0)$ is orthogonal to $u$ , which (since the eigenvalue 0 of $F(0)$ is simple) spans the null space of the transpose matrix $F^{\prime}(0)$ ; hence $v^{\prime}(0)\in\operatorname{ran}(F(0))$ , which implies (by (2.16)–(2.17)) that $v^{\prime}(0)=-QF(0)v^{\prime}(0)$ . Hence (A.7) implies, using also $\lambda(0)=0$ and (A.10),

$$ \displaystyle v^{\prime}(0)=-QF(0)v^{\prime}(0)=-Q\bigl(\lambda^{\prime}(0)v-F^{\prime}(0)v\bigr)=QF^{\prime}(0)v. $$

Differentiate (A.7) again; this yields

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{\prime\prime}(t)v(t)+2\lambda^{\prime}(t)v^{\prime}(t)+\lambda(t)v^{\prime\prime}(t)=F^{\prime\prime}(t)v(t)+2F^{\prime}(t)v^{\prime}(t)+F(t)v^{\prime\prime}(t). $$

Multiplying to the left by $u^{\mathsf{t}}$ yields, using (A.8) and (A.11),

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{\prime\prime}(t)=u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime}(t)v(t)+2u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(t)v^{\prime}(t)+u^{\mathsf{t}}F(t)v^{\prime\prime}(t), $$

which yields (A.2) by taking $t=0$ and using (A.11) and (A.8).

Furthermore, just as for $v^{\prime}(0)$ , (A.8) shows that $v^{\prime\prime}(0)$ is orthogonal to $u$ , and thus $v^{\prime\prime}(0)=-QF(0)v^{\prime\prime}(0)$ . Hence (A.12) implies, using $\lambda(0)=0$ , (A.10), (A.11), and (A.1),

$$ \displaystyle v^{\prime\prime}(0) \displaystyle=-QF(0)v^{\prime\prime}(0)=-2\lambda^{\prime}(0)Qv^{\prime}(0)+Q\bigl(F^{\prime\prime}(0)v(0)+2F^{\prime}(0)v^{\prime}(0)\bigr) \displaystyle=-2(u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(0)v)Q^{2}F^{\prime}(0)v+QF^{\prime\prime}(0)v+2QF^{\prime}(0)QF^{\prime}(0)v. $$

Finally, differentiating (A.13) and taking $t=0$ yields, since $u^{\mathsf{t}}F(0)=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)=u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)v+3u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime\prime}(0)v^{\prime}(0)+3u^{\mathsf{t}}F^{\prime}(0)v^{\prime\prime}(0), $$

and (A.3) follows by substituting (A.11) and (A.14). ∎

## Appendix B Alternative proof of (7.12)

We give here an independent and more “probabilistic” proof of (7.12) in the proof of Theorem 7.2; this proof bypasses the matrix computations of Lemma 7.3.

Let $V_{A}^{B}$ be the number of times that a random walk started from $A$ hits $A$ prior to hitting $B$ (we count the initial state as a hit). By Remark 7.5, the sum $\sum_{m\geqslant 0}W(m)$ in the proof of Theorem 7.2 equals the expectation $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}V_{A}^{B}$ . Recall that the crux of the proof of Theorem 7.2 was to show that this sum is greater than $W(0)=1$ , in other words, that $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}V_{A}^{B}>1$ . We showed this by showing the formula (7.12), which is a special case of Lemma 7.3, proved above by algebraic calculations.

We give here an alternative proof of the following special case of Lemma 7.3, which is sufficient for our use of it in (7.12); the proof uses standard methods and known results for Markov chains. (We guess that similar arguments can be used to prove Lemma 7.3 in general, but we have not pursued this.)

#### Lemma B.1.

Let $P$ be an irreducible stochastic matrix on a finite state space $\mathcal{W}$ , and let $\pi$ be its stationary distribution. Then, for any distinct states $A,B\in\mathcal{W}$ ,

$$ (I-P_{\neq B})_{AA}^{-1}=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}V_{A}^{B}=Q_{AA}-Q_{BA}+(Q_{BB}-Q_{AB}){\frac{\pi_{A}}{\pi_{B}}}. $$

As a first step in the proof, we introduce the random variable

$$ T_{A}^{B}:=\textnormal{time that a walk started from $A$ first visits $A$ after having visited $B$}. $$

#### Lemma B.2.

With the notation defined above,

$$ \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}V_{A}^{B}=\pi_{A}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}T_{A}^{B}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\gamma$ be a random walk starting from $A$ . Define the sequence of random times $T_{0},T_{1},\dots$ as $T_{0}:=0$ and

$$ T_{i}:=\min\{j:j>T_{i-1},\gamma_{j}=A,\gamma_{j^{\prime}}=B\textnormal{ for some }T_{i-1}<j^{\prime}<j\}; $$

in other words, $T_{i}$ is the time of the first return to $A$ after having visited $B$ after $T_{i-1}$ . Since the chain is irreducible and finite, all $T_{i}$ are finite, almost surely. Moreover, by the Markov property, all $T_{i}-T_{i-1}$ are i.i.d. By definition, $T_{1}-T_{0}=T_{1}=T_{A}^{B}$ .

We define associated “rewards” as

$$ V_{i}=\#\{j:0\leqslant j<T_{i}:\gamma_{j}=A\} $$

i.e., the number of visits to $A$ before $T_{i}$ . Similarly to the above, the differences $V_{i}-V_{i-1}$ are i.i.d. by the Markov property. Slightly less obviously, we have $V_{1}-V_{0}=V_{A}^{B}$ . This is because $T_{1}$ is the time of the first visit to $A$ which occurs after the first visit to $B$ . Therefore, any visits to $A$ prior to $T_{1}$ must in fact occur prior to the first visit to $B$ .

By the law of large numbers we thus have, as ${n\to\infty}$ , a.s.,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{T_{n}}{n} \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(T_{i}-T_{i-1})}{n}\to\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}(T_{1}-T_{0})=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}T_{A}^{B}, \displaystyle\frac{V_{n}}{n} \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(V_{i}-V_{i-1})}{n}\to\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}(V_{1}-V_{0})=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}V_{A}^{B}, $$

and thus

$$ \displaystyle\frac{V_{n}}{T_{n}} \displaystyle\to\frac{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}V_{A}^{B}}{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}T_{A}^{B}}. $$

On the other hand, by the Markov chain ergodic theorem, a.s.

$$ \frac{V_{n}}{T_{n}}={\frac{\textnormal{number of visits to $A$ before }T_{n}}{T_{n}}}\to\pi_{A}. $$

Finally, (B.3) follows by comparing (B.8) and (B.9). ∎

#### Proof of Lemma B.1.

The first equality in (B.1) was noted in Remark 7.5. For the second equality, we introduce the mean first passage times $m_{ij}$ . For distinct $i$ and $j$ , $m_{ij}$ is the average number of steps for a walk started at $i$ to reach $j$ for the first time. We define, for convenience, $m_{ii}:=0$ .

We can express $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}T_{A}^{B}$ in terms of the mean first passage times. Indeed, waiting for the first visit to $A$ after passing through $B$ is equivalent to waiting for the first visit to $B$ , and then subsequently waiting for the first visit to $A$ thereafter. So by linearity of expectation,

$$ \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}T_{A}^{B}=m_{AB}+m_{BA}. $$

Combining with Lemma B.2, we thus have

$$ \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}{}V_{A}^{B}=\pi_{A}(m_{AB}+m_{BA}). $$

On the other hand, the mean first passage times are known to be closely related to the entries of the group inverse. More precisely, we have

$$ Q_{ij}=\pi_{j}(\tau^{\prime}_{j}-m_{ij}),\qquad i,j\in\mathcal{W}, $$

where $\tau_{j}^{\prime}:=\sum_{k\neq j}\pi_{k}m_{kj}$ [13, Corollary 11.7]. As a simple consequence,

$$ m_{ij}={\frac{Q_{jj}-Q_{ij}}{\pi_{j}}}. $$

Combining (B.13) with (B.11) yields the second equality in (B.1). ∎
